title: A Guide to White Shaker Kitchens That Last
excerpt: Use this guide to white shaker kitchens to choose cabinet quality, finishes, layouts, hardware, and lighting for a timeless, hardworking Nashville remodel.
content:
A white shaker kitchen can look calm, tailored, and beautifully at home in a historic Belle Meade residence or a busy Franklin family home. But the best results come from more than choosing white doors with a recessed center panel. This guide to white shaker kitchens helps you make the design choices that keep the room feeling intentional, practical, and worth the investment long after the remodel is complete.

White shaker cabinets have staying power because they offer structure without visual heaviness. Their clean lines work with traditional millwork, modern fixtures, warm wood floors, natural stone, and many of the architectural styles found across Middle Tennessee. The trade-off is that a simple cabinet style leaves less room for poor materials, uneven installation, or rushed design decisions to hide.

Why White Shaker Kitchens Continue to Work

Shaker cabinetry is defined by a five-piece door with a flat center panel and straightforward frame. It has enough detail to feel finished, yet it does not compete with the rest of the kitchen. White amplifies that versatility, reflecting light and making a kitchen feel more open.

For homeowners planning to stay in their home, this flexibility matters. You can refresh the personality of a white shaker kitchen over time through paint colors, hardware, lighting, stools, and accessories without replacing the cabinets. That makes it a sensible foundation for a kitchen designed around real life rather than a short-lived trend.

Still, white shaker is not one single look. A bright white paired with polished chrome and marble reads differently than a warmer white with aged brass, oak accents, and honed quartzite. The goal is not to copy a showroom kitchen. It is to select a version of white shaker that belongs in your home and supports the way your household uses the space.

Start With Cabinet Construction, Not Just Door Style

A door sample can make almost any cabinet look appealing. What determines long-term performance is what sits behind it: the cabinet box, joinery, finish, hardware, and installation.

For a high-use family kitchen, plywood cabinet boxes, solid wood face frames where appropriate, quality drawer construction, and soft-close hinges and slides are meaningful upgrades. They help cabinets stay square, drawers operate smoothly, and doors align properly through years of daily use. Fully custom cabinetry also allows for dimensions that fit your room rather than forcing your room to fit standard box sizes.

There are times when a well-selected RTA or stock cabinet line is the right choice. It can shorten lead times and protect more of the budget for countertops, appliances, or a needed layout change. The key is being clear about the compromises. Stock cabinets offer fewer widths, finishes, and modification options, while custom cabinetry offers more precision, storage flexibility, and material choices.

A trustworthy cabinet plan should explain those differences plainly. Homeowners should know what they are paying for, what is included in installation, and where the budget is being allocated before work begins.

Choose a Finish Built for Kitchen Life

White paint should look refined, but it also needs to tolerate fingerprints, cooking residue, and regular cleaning. A factory-applied finish can be an excellent option for consistency. A custom painted finish gives you greater control over color and can coordinate beautifully with existing trim, built-ins, or architectural millwork.

Ask to see samples in the actual kitchen whenever possible. Light changes dramatically between a sunny Nashville afternoon and an evening with interior lighting. A white that appears crisp in a showroom may look blue, gray, or too stark next to your flooring at home.

Warm whites with subtle cream or beige undertones often work well with Tennessee homes that feature honey-toned hardwoods, warm stone, or traditional trim. Cleaner whites can feel fresh and architectural in homes with cooler finishes and generous natural light. There is no universal best white, only the right white for the materials around it.

Plan the Layout Before Selecting the Pretty Details

A beautiful kitchen that creates traffic jams during breakfast or leaves no landing space near the range will not feel luxurious for long. Before finalizing cabinet elevations, consider how people enter the room, where groceries land, who cooks, and where guests tend to gather.

The classic work triangle between the refrigerator, sink, and range remains useful, but modern kitchens often need more than one work zone. A dedicated coffee station can keep morning routines moving. Deep drawers near the range can hold pots and cooking tools. A pantry with adjustable storage can prevent countertop clutter. An island may need seating on one side and hidden storage on the other.

If an existing layout works, keeping plumbing and major appliances near their current locations can reduce renovation cost. If the layout is frustrating every day, moving a wall, widening an opening, or relocating the sink may be the better long-term decision. This is where thoughtful planning protects you from spending money on a kitchen that still does not function the way you need it to.

Storage Should Feel Natural, Not Clever

The most useful storage solutions are usually the ones you do not have to think about. Place dishes near the dishwasher, trash and recycling near food prep, and cooking oils near the range. Deep drawers are often easier to use than lower cabinets with shelves because contents stay visible and accessible.

Custom cabinetry can make awkward corners, narrow walls, and uneven room dimensions work harder. It can also add practical details such as tray dividers, pull-out pantry shelves, spice storage, appliance garages, and drawer organizers. These features should solve an actual household problem, not simply add cost because they look impressive on a design board.

Add Contrast So the Kitchen Does Not Feel Flat

White shaker cabinets are a neutral starting point, not a complete design. Without contrast and texture, the room can feel sterile. Countertops, backsplash, hardware, flooring, and lighting give the kitchen its depth.

A natural wood island is a warm choice for homeowners who want a furniture-like focal point. A painted island in soft charcoal, muted green, or deep navy can create contrast while still feeling timeless. If the room is already compact, keeping the island white may preserve a more open appearance, while texture in the backsplash or wood tones can provide the needed variation.

For countertops, quartz offers easy maintenance and a wide range of subtle patterns. Natural stone brings character and variation, though some materials require more care. A simple backsplash lets cabinet details and countertops lead; a handmade or lightly textured tile adds warmth when the other surfaces are restrained.

Hardware is the finishing touch that changes the mood quickly. Brushed nickel is versatile and familiar. Unlacquered or aged brass brings warmth but develops character over time. Matte black can add definition, particularly when repeated in lighting or plumbing fixtures. Before committing, view the finish beside the cabinet sample, countertop, and backsplash rather than choosing it in isolation.

Give Lighting the Same Attention as Cabinetry

A white kitchen needs layered light to feel welcoming after sunset. Recessed ceiling lights provide general illumination, but they should not be the only source. Under-cabinet lighting improves food preparation and gives the backsplash a soft evening glow. Pendants over an island add personality and help define the center of the room.

Color temperature matters. Many homeowners prefer warm white lighting around 2700K to 3000K because it flatters white cabinetry, wood accents, and skin tones. Cooler light can make some white finishes look clinical. Dimmers are a small addition with a major payoff, allowing the kitchen to shift from weekday task space to relaxed gathering place.

Budget for the Details That Protect the Finished Look

Cabinets are a central investment, but a realistic kitchen budget also accounts for demolition, electrical work, plumbing, countertops, backsplash, flooring, paint, appliance installation, and possible repairs behind the walls. Older homes can reveal surprises once construction begins, so a sensible contingency is part of responsible planning.

The least expensive option is not always the most affordable over time. Poorly fitted filler panels, misaligned doors, low-quality hinges, and rushed trim work can make even a beautiful cabinet style look unfinished. Precise installation is what turns individual components into a kitchen that feels built for the home.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, the conversation starts with your priorities: what must change, what can stay, and where craftsmanship will make the biggest difference within your budget. Clear scope and careful planning help replace remodeling uncertainty with confidence before the first cabinet is installed.

A White Shaker Kitchen Should Feel Like Yours

The strongest white shaker kitchens do not rely on a trend cycle or a single perfect product. They pair durable cabinetry with a layout that respects daily routines, finishes that complement the home, and details that make people want to linger at the island. When each choice is made with care, the result is more than a bright new kitchen. It is a room where weekday mornings run easier, family meals feel more comfortable, and you can genuinely fall in love with your home again.

title: How to Prepare for Cabinet Installation Properly
excerpt: Learn how to prepare for cabinet installation with a clear homeowner checklist for measurements, access, utilities, schedules, and a clean, ready space at home.
content:
A cabinet installation day should feel organized, not disruptive. The best way to protect your timeline, your home, and your investment is to know how to prepare for cabinet installation before the crew arrives. A few thoughtful decisions ahead of time help prevent last-minute surprises, give installers room to work precisely, and bring you closer to a kitchen or bath that feels made for the way your family lives.

Cabinets are not simply placed against a wall. Proper installation depends on accurate measurements, level surfaces, clear access, and coordination with flooring, appliances, plumbing, electrical work, and countertops. Whether you have chosen fully custom cabinetry or a budget-conscious stock cabinet solution, preparation is where a smooth project begins.

Confirm the Final Plan Before Materials Arrive

Before installation day, review the approved cabinet plan with your contractor or designer. This is the time to confirm cabinet locations, door styles, hardware, finishes, appliance openings, and special features such as pullout organizers, appliance garages, wine storage, or a built-in range hood surround.

Small changes can have a large effect once cabinets are ordered or on site. Moving a sink base, changing the width of a refrigerator opening, or adding a microwave drawer may affect electrical, plumbing, ventilation, trim, and countertop layouts. If something no longer fits your routine or your vision, speak up early. Clear decisions before installation protect both your schedule and your budget.

It also helps to ask what is included in the installation scope. For example, cabinet installation may be scheduled separately from countertop templating, backsplash tile, painting, appliance hookups, or final hardware installation. Knowing the sequence keeps expectations clear and helps you plan for the temporary inconvenience of having an unfinished kitchen.

Clear the Room and Create a Safe Work Zone

Your installers need more than an empty countertop. They need safe, open paths to carry cabinets, tools, and materials through the home without risking damage to walls, furniture, or the cabinetry itself.

Remove everything from existing cabinets, drawers, pantry shelves, and nearby closets that may be affected by the work. Pack dishes, small appliances, food, cleaning supplies, and personal items before demolition or installation begins. Keep essentials in clearly marked bins so you can find what you need while your kitchen is out of service.

Move freestanding furniture, rugs, wall décor, and breakable items away from the work area and the route from the entry door to the room. If a dining room, hallway, or living space will be used for staging materials, clear that space as well. Your project team may use floor protection, but removing obstacles is still one of the simplest ways to prevent accidents.

If children or pets live in the home, establish boundaries before work starts. Installation involves sharp tools, heavy components, open doorways, dust, and frequent movement in and out of the house. A separate, comfortable area for pets and a clear rule about the work zone can make the day safer and less stressful for everyone.

Make Access Easy for the Installation Crew

Cabinets are large, heavy, and often delivered in multiple boxes or assembled pieces. Before the scheduled date, make sure the driveway, walkway, and closest entry point are accessible. Move vehicles if they block loading or unloading, unlock gates, and trim back any low branches that interfere with the path.

Inside, measure the practical route into the room if access is tight. Narrow halls, low stairwells, sharp turns, and small door openings can affect how cabinetry is carried inside. Your cabinet professional will typically evaluate access during planning, but let them know if anything has changed since the site visit.

Plan for a responsible adult to be available at the start of the workday. That person should be able to answer questions, confirm access, and make timely decisions if an unexpected site condition appears. You do not need to hover over the crew, but being reachable avoids delays when a question requires homeowner approval.

Finish the Behind-the-Wall Work First

Cabinets cover walls, plumbing lines, and portions of the floor, so the room should be ready before they go in. Any required rough plumbing, electrical updates, HVAC adjustments, gas-line work, wall repairs, or structural changes should be completed and inspected before cabinet installation begins.

This step matters especially in older Nashville-area homes, where walls and floors may not be perfectly straight or level. An experienced installer can scribe and fit cabinetry for a refined appearance, but unresolved framing, moisture damage, or uneven subfloor issues should be addressed first. Cabinets should not be used to hide an active problem.

Confirm the location of outlet boxes, switches, water shutoffs, drain lines, and appliance connections against the final plan. A dishwasher needs the right opening and connections. A range may require a specific electrical circuit or gas location. An island may need power for outlets, lighting, or charging drawers. Once cabinetry is installed, relocating these elements becomes more complicated and expensive.

Never ask an installer to work around active leaks, exposed wiring, or an unapproved gas connection. Those conditions deserve attention from the appropriate licensed professional before cabinetry is set.

Check Floors, Walls, and Ceiling Details

One of the most common homeowner questions is whether flooring should go in before or after cabinets. The answer depends on the material, the project design, and the condition of the room.

Many remodels install permanent cabinets before certain finished floors, particularly when using flooring that should not be trapped under heavy cabinet boxes. Other projects install flooring first for a continuous appearance or because of an existing layout. There is no one-size-fits-all rule. The right sequence should be decided before installation so cabinet heights, dishwasher clearance, toe kicks, and transitions are all planned correctly.

Walls should be dry, reasonably smooth, and ready for cabinets. Complete major patching, priming, and painting that would be difficult behind cabinetry. If you are adding decorative ceiling beams, crown molding, or a statement range hood, make sure those details have been coordinated with cabinet height and crown dimensions.

Do not worry if your home is not perfectly square. Very few are. Quality installation accounts for real-world conditions through careful shimming, leveling, fastening, and finish work. What matters is identifying unusual conditions early rather than discovering them with a cabinet in hand.

Protect Your Routine While the Room Is Offline

A kitchen remodel affects daily life more than almost any other interior project. Set up a temporary kitchen before your current kitchen is dismantled. A coffee maker, microwave, toaster oven, paper goods, water station, and a small selection of pantry staples can make the transition much easier.

Choose a location away from dust and construction traffic, such as a dining room, laundry room, basement, or covered outdoor space when weather allows. Keep your temporary setup simple. This is not the week to attempt elaborate meals or store every dish within reach.

You should also plan for noise, dust, and limited access. Even with careful containment and cleanup practices, cabinet installation is active work. If you work from home, schedule calls away from the work zone. If you have a major gathering planned, consider whether the project calendar leaves enough cushion for the unexpected. A well-planned renovation is predictable, but weather, inspections, material deliveries, and hidden conditions can still influence timing.

Inspect Materials Without Creating Delays

When cabinets arrive, your project team will generally inspect them for visible damage and compare them to the order. Homeowners can help by providing a clean, dry staging area and avoiding the temptation to open every package or move components around.

If you notice a concern, document it and notify your contractor promptly. A finish variation, a missing part, or transit damage is best handled before the installation is too far along. At the same time, do not assume every separate panel or unfinished edge is an error. Fillers, end panels, toe-kick pieces, trim, and scribe material often look different before the cabinetry is assembled and finished in place.

Save Final Decisions for the Walkthrough

As installation nears completion, a final walkthrough gives you the opportunity to review door and drawer alignment, hardware placement, trim details, cabinet operation, and overall fit. This is the right time to ask questions about care, cleaning, touch-ups, and what comes next for countertops or other finishing trades.

Avoid using new cabinets as storage until the crew confirms they are ready. Fresh adjustments, final fastening, and cleanup are easier when drawers and shelves are empty. Once the room is complete, take a moment to appreciate the details that made the project feel personal: the right pantry layout, the drawer that finally holds your pots, the island designed for homework and weekend conversations.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, careful preparation is part of the craftsmanship. A clear plan and a ready home give every cabinet, detail, and finish the chance to look its best – and give you more confidence from the first installation day onward.

title: Cabinet Hardware That Makes Your Kitchen Feel Finished
excerpt: Choose cabinet hardware that fits your style, budget, and daily routine. Learn finishes, sizing, placement, and details that make cabinetry feel complete.
content:
A kitchen can have beautifully built cabinets, fresh counters, and the right lighting, yet still feel unfinished when the cabinet hardware is an afterthought. Knobs, pulls, hinges, and latches are the parts you touch every day. They influence how your kitchen works, how it wears over time, and whether the finished room feels thoughtfully designed or pieced together.

For homeowners in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, and throughout Middle Tennessee, hardware is also one of the most effective ways to give a kitchen a more personal, elevated look without changing the entire cabinet plan. The right choice should feel good in your hand, suit the scale of the cabinetry, and support the way your household actually uses the room.

Why Cabinet Hardware Matters More Than You Think

Cabinet hardware is often described as the jewelry of the kitchen, but it does more than add polish. A pull that is too small can make wide drawers awkward to open. A finish that clashes with the faucet or lighting can make an otherwise cohesive room feel unsettled. Low-quality hinges can lead to doors that sag, bang, or need frequent adjustment.

Good hardware brings together the practical and visual sides of a remodel. It makes heavy drawers easier to use, protects cabinet finishes from fingerprints around door edges, and creates a rhythm across the room. In a busy family kitchen, those small improvements are felt every morning, every dinner rush, and every time friends gather around the island.

The best choice is not always the most expensive one. It is the one that matches the cabinet style, holds up to daily use, and fits comfortably within the overall project budget. That is why hardware deserves attention early in the design process, rather than becoming a rushed decision near installation day.

Start With the Style of Your Cabinets

Hardware should complement the cabinets, not compete with them. The door profile, wood species, paint color, and overall architecture of the home all help narrow the field.

Flat-panel or shaker cabinets are remarkably flexible. Long bar pulls can give them a tailored, contemporary appearance, while rounded knobs and cup pulls create a warmer, more traditional feel. In a classic Nashville home, brushed brass or aged bronze can bring character to painted cabinetry without making the room feel overly formal.

Slab-front cabinets tend to look best with clean, minimal hardware. Slim pulls, edge pulls, or carefully selected knobs preserve the quiet lines of the design. Ornate pieces can work, but they need to be intentional. Too much detail on a simple cabinet front can make the kitchen feel busy.

For raised-panel, inset, or more traditional custom cabinetry, hardware with gentle curves, texture, or a historic influence can add depth. Think substantial knobs, bin pulls, or softly shaped handles rather than highly angular bars. The goal is not to recreate a period kitchen exactly. It is to choose details that feel appropriate to the home and will still feel right years from now.

A mixed approach can also work beautifully. Many kitchens use knobs on upper doors and pulls on lower doors and drawers. This gives the room variation while keeping operation easy. The key is selecting pieces from the same finish family and visual style so the combination looks planned.

Choose Cabinet Hardware That Fits Your Hands and Your Drawers

A hardware sample may look perfect on a showroom board but feel entirely different once it is mounted on a full-size drawer. Comfort matters, especially in kitchens with deep pots-and-pans drawers, pullout trash cabinets, or large pantry doors.

For drawers, pulls are usually the practical choice. They give you more grip and distribute force across the drawer front. Wider drawers generally need longer pulls, two pulls, or a more substantial style that looks balanced. A tiny knob centered on a wide drawer can appear lost and may be frustrating to use when the drawer is loaded.

There is no single measurement that works for every kitchen, but proportion is a useful guide. A pull often looks balanced when its length is roughly one-third of the drawer width. On very wide drawers, two pulls may create a more symmetrical look and make opening easier. If you prefer a clean, modern appearance, a single longer pull can be the better choice.

For cabinet doors, knobs work well on smaller doors and lighter-use areas. Pulls are often easier for tall pantry doors, refrigerator panels, and heavy cabinet doors. Before committing, hold several samples. Make sure fingers do not hit the cabinet face behind the pull and that the grip feels comfortable for everyone in the home.

Placement matters just as much as size. On shaker doors, hardware is commonly positioned near the corner where the stile and rail meet. On drawers, it is usually centered. Those conventions create a clean appearance, but they are not rules that should override function. Tall cabinets, appliance panels, and specialty storage often benefit from a custom placement plan.

Select a Finish That Works With the Whole Room

Hardware finishes do not have to exactly match every metal in the kitchen. In fact, a space can feel more collected and welcoming when it includes two complementary finishes. What matters is that the combination feels deliberate.

Brushed nickel remains a dependable choice because it is versatile, understated, and forgiving of everyday fingerprints. Matte black creates contrast on white, natural wood, and light gray cabinetry, especially in transitional or modern kitchens. Polished chrome offers a brighter, more classic look and pairs naturally with many stainless appliances.

Warm metals such as brushed brass, champagne bronze, and antique brass bring richness to painted cabinets and can soften a room with stone, tile, and cooler colors. Their trade-off is visibility: some living finishes develop character over time, while others show marks more readily. If a perfectly uniform appearance is important, select a finish designed for consistency and ask about its expected maintenance needs.

When mixing metals, choose one finish to lead and one to support it. For example, a kitchen might use warm brass hardware with a black faucet or black lighting accents. Repeating each finish at least once helps the room feel connected. Trying to include too many unrelated metals can make selection feel accidental instead of refined.

Do Not Overlook Hinges, Drawer Slides, and Latches

Visible knobs and pulls receive the most attention, but concealed cabinet hardware has a major impact on daily comfort. Soft-close hinges prevent doors from slamming and protect both the cabinet box and the peace of the home. Full-extension drawer slides allow you to reach the back of a drawer without digging through its contents.

These details are especially worthwhile in a kitchen designed for real life. A well-built drawer should open smoothly even when it is loaded with dishes, cookware, or pantry staples. Heavy-duty slides may cost more than standard options, but they make sense for deep drawers and frequently used storage.

Specialty hardware can solve common frustrations as well. Pullout trash systems keep waste out of sight. Tray dividers organize baking sheets and cutting boards. Swing-out pantry storage can make better use of narrow spaces. These upgrades should be chosen based on your routines, not simply because they look impressive in a display kitchen.

Plan Hardware Before Installation Day

Hardware changes are easy to picture but surprisingly hard to reverse once holes have been drilled. A clear selection plan prevents last-minute substitutions, mismatched finishes, and placement decisions made under pressure.

Begin by identifying the hardware style and finish, then confirm the exact quantity needed for every door, drawer, panel, and specialty cabinet. Order a few samples before purchasing the full set. Place them against the actual cabinet color, countertop, backsplash, and nearby lighting. A finish that looks warm in a store may read very differently under the lighting in your home.

It is also wise to account for lead times and replacement availability. If a handle is damaged years from now, a widely available collection may be easier to match than a limited-run piece. For a custom kitchen, a cabinetry professional can create a placement layout before installation so every pull and knob aligns properly across the room.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, those details are considered as part of the larger plan, not left to chance. The goal is a finished kitchen with cabinetry, millwork, storage, and hardware working together within a scope that respects your home and your budget.

The right hardware will not just photograph well on the day your remodel is complete. It will feel natural in your hand on an ordinary Tuesday morning, make daily tasks easier, and add one more reason to enjoy gathering in a kitchen that finally feels like yours.

title: Ready to Assemble Cabinets Review: Are They Worth It?
excerpt: Our ready to assemble cabinets review explains quality, cost, installation, and when RTA cabinets are a smart fit for a Nashville kitchen remodel project
content:
A kitchen remodel can feel expensive before a single cabinet door comes off. That is why a ready to assemble cabinets review deserves more than a quick verdict. RTA cabinets can be a smart, attractive way to update a Nashville kitchen on a more controlled budget, but the right result depends on the cabinet construction, the layout, and who assembles and installs them.

For many homeowners in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, and Belle Meade, the question is not simply, “Are RTA cabinets good?” It is whether they will look polished, work well for a busy household, and hold up over time. The honest answer is that some do. Others create the very remodeling headaches homeowners hoped to avoid.

What Ready to Assemble Cabinets Actually Mean

Ready to assemble cabinets arrive in boxed components rather than as fully built cabinet boxes. The doors, drawer fronts, sides, shelves, and hardware are packaged for assembly before installation. Because manufacturers can ship flat-packed cabinets more efficiently and reduce factory labor, RTA options usually cost less than assembled stock cabinetry or fully custom work.

That lower price is real, but it should not be confused with one universal level of quality. “RTA” describes how cabinets are shipped, not how they are made. One line may use furniture-grade plywood boxes, solid wood doors, dovetail drawers, and soft-close hardware. Another may rely heavily on particleboard, thin drawer bottoms, stapled joints, and finishes that do not stand up well to kitchen traffic.

This distinction matters. A cabinet may look beautiful in a photo yet disappoint once it is carrying dinnerware, supporting a heavy countertop, or facing daily use from kids, guests, and pets.

Ready to Assemble Cabinets Review: The Real Benefits

The strongest RTA cabinet lines offer homeowners a practical middle ground. They can provide a clean, updated kitchen without requiring the investment level of fully custom cabinetry. For a straightforward kitchen footprint, that can free up budget for better countertops, lighting, appliances, or a more thoughtful backsplash.

Cost predictability is another advantage. With a clear cabinet plan and a verified order, homeowners can understand the cabinet portion of the budget early in the process. That is especially helpful when remodeling a home that needs several improvements at once.

RTA cabinetry also often comes in popular, timeless styles. Shaker doors, painted whites and warm neutrals, stained woods, and simple transitional profiles fit many Middle Tennessee homes. When selected carefully and professionally installed, these cabinets can look far more refined than their boxed delivery method suggests.

Lead times can be favorable as well. Custom cabinets are built specifically for your home, which is worth the wait when the design calls for it. But for homeowners who want a faster refresh with a dependable layout, quality RTA cabinetry may be available sooner.

Where RTA Cabinets Can Fall Short

The trade-off is flexibility. Stock RTA cabinets come in predetermined widths, heights, and depths. If your kitchen has an awkward corner, an off-center window, uneven walls, or a space that needs an exact-size pantry, standard boxes may leave gaps or require filler panels. Good design can make these details look intentional. Poor planning makes them obvious.

Finish consistency is another consideration. Cabinet doors and panels should match closely, particularly in painted colors and wood tones. Ordering from a reputable manufacturer helps, but a skilled installer should inspect every piece before the project reaches its final stage.

Assembly is also more demanding than it appears. A cabinet box that is even slightly out of square can affect door alignment, drawer operation, and countertop installation. The work requires level surfaces, patience, the right tools, and a clear understanding of cabinet construction. Saving money by assembling cabinets yourself can make sense for an experienced DIY homeowner with time to spare. For most kitchen remodels, professional assembly and installation protect the investment.

Finally, RTA cabinets do not offer unlimited personalization. You may find the right door style but not the exact depth needed for a small appliance garage. You may want a range hood surround, integrated refrigerator panels, or custom storage that stock components cannot fully accommodate. That is where a blended approach can be especially effective.

How to Judge Cabinet Quality Before You Buy

Do not let a door sample make the entire decision. Ask what is behind the door and inside the drawer. Cabinet construction affects how the kitchen performs long after the excitement of remodel day has passed.

Look for plywood cabinet boxes rather than thin particleboard where possible, particularly around sink bases and high-use areas. Plywood generally offers better screw-holding strength and moisture resistance. Solid wood door frames, quality panel construction, full-extension drawer glides, and soft-close hinges are all signs that a line is built for regular use.

Drawer construction deserves close attention. Dovetail joinery is a strong indicator of quality, though it is not the only factor. Examine the drawer bottom thickness, glide capacity, and how smoothly it opens when loaded. A kitchen drawer should hold cookware and utensils without wobbling or binding.

Also ask about the finish. A durable factory-applied finish usually performs better than a thin coating prone to chipping around edges. In a family kitchen, cabinet finishes need to tolerate fingerprints, cleaning, chair bumps, and the occasional dropped pan.

Measurements are equally important. Before ordering, verify walls, windows, doors, ceiling height, appliance specifications, plumbing locations, and flooring changes. Cabinet mistakes are costly because they can delay every trade that follows. A clear design plan is not an extra step. It is what keeps the project moving.

When RTA Is the Right Choice

RTA cabinetry is often a strong choice when the room has a relatively standard layout, the homeowner wants a meaningful visual upgrade, and the budget calls for smart priorities. It works well for a kitchen refresh, rental property, secondary kitchen, laundry room, bathroom, or a remodel where quality stock cabinetry allows more room for other improvements.

It is also a sensible option when you have professional guidance. The best outcomes do not come from clicking through cabinet sizes and hoping they fit. They come from a plan that accounts for function, traffic flow, appliance clearances, storage needs, and the details that make a room feel finished.

For example, a homeowner may choose RTA perimeter cabinets in a classic painted finish, then add custom panels, trim, floating shelves, or a tailored island feature. This approach can deliver a custom-looking kitchen while keeping the overall budget more comfortable.

When Custom Cabinetry Is Worth the Investment

Custom cabinetry becomes the better choice when the home calls for exact proportions or a more personal design. Older Nashville homes often have walls that are not perfectly straight, unusual corners, low windows, or architectural features worth preserving. Custom work allows the cabinetry to fit the home rather than forcing the home to fit standard boxes.

It is also ideal for homeowners who want specialized storage, distinctive finishes, inset construction, furniture-style details, or architectural millwork that ties the kitchen to the rest of the house. If you are renovating a kitchen you expect to enjoy for decades, the ability to tailor every dimension can be worth it.

The decision does not have to be all or nothing. A thoughtful designer can help identify where custom craftsmanship will have the greatest visual and functional impact, while using quality stock options where they make practical sense.

Installation Is What Makes Cabinets Feel Finished

Even excellent cabinets can look disappointing if they are installed poorly. Cabinet runs must be level, plumb, securely fastened, and carefully scribed to walls. Doors and drawers need final adjustment. Fillers, trim, end panels, crown molding, and toe kicks should create a cohesive appearance rather than looking like afterthoughts.

This is where homeowners often see the biggest difference between a cabinet purchase and a completed kitchen. The cabinet boxes are only part of the result. Precise installation turns them into a room that feels calm, tailored, and ready for real life.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, the goal is to help homeowners choose the level of cabinetry that fits both their home and their budget, then carry the project through with clear planning and careful workmanship. Whether the right answer is quality RTA cabinets, fully custom cabinetry, or a combination of both, the best choice is the one that gives you confidence every time you walk into your kitchen.

A well-planned cabinet remodel should leave you with more than new storage. It should give you a kitchen that makes weekday mornings easier, brings people together comfortably, and feels like it has always belonged in your home.

title: Kitchen Cabinet Organizers That Work Harder
excerpt: Kitchen cabinet organizers turn crowded storage into a calm, efficient workspace. See which solutions fit your cooking habits, budget, and cabinet layout.
content:
A beautiful kitchen can still feel frustrating when the cookware is stacked three deep, the spices disappear behind bottles, and the trash pullout is always in the way. The right kitchen cabinet organizers solve those daily annoyances at the source. They make the room easier to cook in, easier to clean, and more enjoyable to share with family and guests.

For homeowners planning a kitchen update in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, or Belle Meade, organization should not be an afterthought. It works best when it is considered alongside cabinet layout, appliance placement, and the way your household actually uses the kitchen. A well-designed cabinet is not just attractive from the outside. It gives every hardworking item a practical place to live.

Start With How Your Kitchen Really Works

The best organizer is not necessarily the one with the most features. It is the one that removes a repeated frustration from your day. Think about what happens when you make coffee in the morning, pack lunches, prepare a weeknight dinner, or clean up after company. Those routines reveal where storage is falling short.

A household that cooks often may benefit most from deep drawers near the range, divided storage for utensils, and a pullout pantry for ingredients. Someone who entertains may prefer dedicated space for serving pieces, wine glasses, or platters that are awkward to stack. If baking is a regular part of your routine, heavy mixers and sheet pans deserve a home that does not require lifting, digging, or rearranging.

Before choosing hardware or accessories, take a close look at what you own. Keep the tools you use, donate what no longer earns its space, and measure the larger items that need a dependable home. This simple step prevents a common mistake: installing a beautiful organizer that is the wrong size for the things it is meant to hold.

Kitchen Cabinet Organizers That Earn Their Space

Some storage solutions make a dramatic difference in almost any kitchen. Others are highly specific to the homeowner. The right mix depends on cabinet dimensions, budget, and whether you are updating existing cabinetry or designing a new kitchen from the ground up.

Deep drawers for pots, pans, and everyday dishes

Lower cabinets with fixed shelves often turn into dark, hard-to-reach storage. Deep drawers bring the contents forward, so you can see a skillet, Dutch oven, or stack of plates without kneeling and reaching into the back of the cabinet.

They are especially useful below a cooktop or near a dishwasher. With the right drawer construction and quality slides, deep drawers can handle substantial weight while opening smoothly. For many families, replacing one or two difficult base cabinets with drawers delivers more daily value than adding another decorative feature.

Rollout shelves for existing base cabinets

If a full renovation is not in the plan, rollout shelves can make a traditional base cabinet far more functional. They bring cans, small appliances, and food storage containers out into the open. This is a practical choice for homeowners who like their current cabinet style but want less bending and searching.

There is a trade-off. Rollout shelves improve access, but they still work within the opening and capacity of the existing cabinet. A newly designed drawer base usually offers a cleaner, more tailored solution. Still, quality rollouts can be a smart investment when a targeted upgrade is the goal.

Vertical dividers for trays and boards

Cookie sheets, cutting boards, cooling racks, and serving trays are notorious for creating a leaning tower in one crowded cabinet. Vertical dividers create individual slots so each item can be pulled out without an avalanche.

This organizer is most useful in a narrow cabinet near the oven or prep area. It does not need much room, but it saves time every time you reach for a sheet pan. It is one of those small details that makes a kitchen feel intentionally designed for real life.

Pullout pantry storage

A tall pantry pullout keeps dry goods visible from both sides and makes better use of narrow spaces. Instead of losing ingredients in the back of a deep pantry, you can scan the contents quickly and keep categories together.

A pullout pantry is not always the right answer, however. Large families or bulk shoppers may need the capacity of a walk-in pantry or wide pantry cabinet with adjustable shelves. Pullouts offer exceptional access, but the overall storage volume and weight limits should match the way you shop.

Waste and recycling pullouts

A dedicated waste pullout is one of the most requested features in a functional kitchen. Placed near the primary prep zone, it keeps trash and recycling contained while making cleanup easier. It also eliminates the visual clutter of a freestanding bin.

The key is choosing the right location. Putting the trash pullout too close to a busy walkway can create congestion when one person is cooking and another is passing through. During the design stage, think about where food is prepped, where dishes are cleared, and how doors and drawers will open at the same time.

Drawer dividers and specialty inserts

Shallow drawers can become catchalls quickly. Adjustable dividers provide a simple home for flatware, cooking utensils, knives, spices, and food storage lids. They are not flashy, but they support the everyday order that makes a kitchen feel calm.

Custom inserts offer a more polished fit and can be designed around your exact drawer dimensions and collection of tools. They cost more than basic adjustable trays, yet they can be worth it in the drawers you use constantly. A knife block insert near the prep area, for example, keeps sharp blades protected, accessible, and off the countertop.

Plan Storage by Zone, Not by Cabinet

A kitchen functions best when storage follows the work being done in each area. This approach is more useful than simply trying to fill every empty cabinet with an accessory.

Near the cooking zone, keep pots, pans, utensils, oils, and spices within easy reach. In the prep zone, prioritize knives, cutting boards, mixing bowls, and access to trash. The cleanup zone should support dishes, glassware, dishwasher loading, and cleaning supplies. The pantry zone should make everyday ingredients simple to find before the grocery list gets out of hand.

This is where thoughtful cabinetry design matters. Cabinet organizers cannot fully fix a layout that puts the essentials in the wrong places. But when organizers and cabinet placement are planned together, the kitchen starts to feel natural almost immediately.

Choose Quality Where It Gets Used Most

Not every organizer requires a custom solution. Simple drawer dividers and shelf risers can be effective budget-conscious additions. The places worth investing in are the ones that carry weight, move constantly, or affect your kitchen workflow every day.

Look for sturdy drawer boxes, reliable full-extension slides, properly secured pullout mechanisms, and materials that can stand up to spills and regular use. A bargain accessory that sticks, sags, or loosens after a year is not a savings. Quality hardware creates the quiet, dependable experience homeowners expect from a well-built kitchen.

For a full remodel, custom cabinetry allows organizers to be built into the design rather than fitted in later. That can mean drawers sized for your cookware, a charging drawer that keeps cords out of sight, or a concealed appliance garage that clears the counter without making daily access difficult. Stock and RTA cabinetry can also be organized effectively, though the available sizes and accessory options may be more limited.

Avoid Organizing for Someone Else’s Lifestyle

Design magazines can make specialty storage look essential, but a kitchen should reflect the people who live there. A wine rack is wasted space for a family that does not collect wine. A large spice pullout may be less useful than wide drawers for someone who relies on simple meals and bulk pantry staples.

Ask yourself four honest questions before committing to a storage feature:

  • What do we reach for every day?
  • What currently creates the most clutter or frustration?
  • Who uses this kitchen, and what can they comfortably access?
  • Will this feature still serve us well in five years?

Those answers lead to practical choices and help keep the budget focused on features that improve daily life. The goal is not to add organizers everywhere. It is to create a kitchen where opening a cabinet feels easy, predictable, and satisfying.

A well-organized kitchen gives you back small moments throughout the day: a quicker dinner start, a clearer counter, less searching, and more room to enjoy the people gathered around the island. When planning cabinetry, let your real routines guide the details. The best storage is the kind you barely notice because it simply works.

title: How to Choose a Custom Bathroom Vanity for You
excerpt: Learn how to choose custom bathroom vanity cabinetry that fits your space, routine, and budget, with practical guidance for Middle Tennessee homes today.
content:
A bathroom vanity may occupy only one wall, but it carries much of the room’s daily workload. It has to make rushed weekday mornings easier, keep countertops under control, stand up to moisture, and still feel right when guests visit. Knowing how to choose custom bathroom vanity cabinetry starts with looking beyond a pretty door style. The best choice is one that fits the room, the people who use it, and the level of investment you want to make in your home.

For homeowners in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, and throughout Middle Tennessee, a custom vanity can solve the problems that off-the-shelf options often leave behind: an awkward gap beside the wall, shallow drawers, wasted corner space, or a finish that does not match the rest of the home. The goal is not simply to fill a space. It is to create a bathroom that feels calmer, more useful, and built for real life.

Start With How the Bathroom Is Actually Used

Before choosing wood species, hardware, or countertop color, consider who uses the room and what creates frustration now. A primary bathroom used by two adults has different demands than a powder room or a child’s shared bath. One might need dedicated storage for grooming tools, cosmetics, and extra towels. Another may only need a handsome cabinet with enough room for hand soap and a few essentials.

Think about the habits that happen in front of the vanity. If two people are routinely getting ready at the same time, a double-sink layout may be worthwhile. If one person uses the space most of the time, a generous single sink can leave more continuous countertop space and simplify the plumbing. More sinks are not always better. They reduce drawer and cabinet space below, and in a narrow room, they can make the vanity feel crowded.

Storage should follow what you own, not what looks good in a showroom. Deep drawers can handle folded towels and hair tools. Shallow top drawers with organizers keep smaller items from disappearing. A pull-out outlet drawer can make room for electric toothbrushes and grooming tools without leaving cords on the counter. These are small details, but they can make a bathroom feel noticeably more organized every day.

Measure the Room Before You Fall for a Style

A custom vanity gives you flexibility, but it does not eliminate the physical limits of the room. Accurate measurements are the foundation of a good design. Measure wall-to-wall dimensions, but also account for door swings, shower doors, toilet clearance, heating vents, baseboards, and windowsills.

Pay particular attention to these four dimensions:

  • Available width, including whether the vanity should run wall to wall or leave breathing room at either side
  • Desired depth, which is often about 21 inches but may need to be reduced in a tight bathroom
  • Finished counter height, typically around 34 to 36 inches depending on the sink and household preferences
  • Clear walking space in front of the vanity, especially when drawers or cabinet doors are open

A vanity that looks substantial in a large primary bath can overwhelm a compact hall bathroom. Conversely, a vanity that is too small can leave valuable storage unused. Custom cabinetry makes it possible to use unusual widths and depths wisely, but thoughtful proportions still matter.

Consider Plumbing and Electrical Early

Moving plumbing can expand your layout options, but it also affects cost and project scope. Keeping sinks near existing supply and drain lines is often the most budget-conscious route. If a better layout requires changes, it is worth discussing those trade-offs early, before cabinetry is designed and ordered.

The same applies to electrical planning. Decide where sconces, outlets, switches, and charging stations belong before finalizing the vanity. A beautifully built cabinet should support the way the entire bathroom functions, not force last-minute compromises.

Choose Materials That Can Handle Bathroom Conditions

Bathrooms deal with humidity, splashes, damp towels, and frequent cleaning. Material selection should reflect that reality. A vanity does not need to look utilitarian to perform well, but it does need construction and finishes that are suited to a moisture-prone room.

Solid wood cabinetry offers warmth, strength, and a distinctive furniture-quality feel. It is an excellent choice for homeowners who want a truly tailored look, especially when the vanity will be a focal point in a primary bathroom or powder room. Quality wood construction also allows for precise detailing, from inset doors to custom drawer configurations and decorative legs.

That said, wood naturally responds to changes in humidity. Proper sealing, quality joinery, and a well-managed bathroom environment help it perform beautifully over time. Painted finishes are popular for their versatility, while stained wood can highlight natural grain and bring depth to the space. In either case, choose a finish designed to stand up to moisture and routine cleaning.

Some projects benefit from a combination of materials. For example, a painted custom vanity may pair with a durable quartz countertop, porcelain tile flooring, and polished nickel hardware for a refined, low-maintenance result. The best material decision is rarely about choosing the most expensive option. It is about choosing the right level of durability and detail for the room’s use and your long-term plans for the home.

Design Storage Around the Countertop You Want to Keep Clear

A clear countertop makes a bathroom feel larger and more peaceful. Achieving that look depends less on self-discipline than on whether every daily item has a sensible home.

Start by identifying what must live near the sink. Hair dryers, brushes, skincare, makeup, medications, contact supplies, and extra toilet paper all need different types of storage. Drawers are generally more accessible than deep lower cabinets because they bring contents forward instead of making you reach into the back. A mix of deep and shallow drawers often gives the best result.

Do not overlook the sink cabinet. Plumbing takes up valuable room, but thoughtful construction can still create useful storage around it. Custom configurations can incorporate U-shaped drawers, narrow side drawers, or pull-out trays that make better use of space that standard cabinets waste.

For a powder room, storage needs may be modest, but the visual impact is high. This is a good place to consider a furniture-style vanity, a statement finish, or a distinctive countertop. Because guests use the room, it should feel intentional, while still providing the practical basics.

Match the Vanity Style to the Home, Not Just the Trend

A vanity should feel connected to the rest of your home. In a traditional Belle Meade residence, warm stained wood, framed doors, and classic hardware may feel natural. In a newer Franklin home, clean-lined cabinetry with a painted finish and simple pulls may better suit the architecture. A transitional design often works especially well because it balances timeless proportions with current finishes.

Trends can offer inspiration, but they should not drive every decision. A bold color may be perfect for a small powder room where you want personality. In a large primary bathroom, a quieter finish might offer more longevity and make future updates easier. If you love a current look, use it in lighting, mirrors, wallpaper, or hardware rather than making it the most permanent element of the room.

Door style also changes the character of the vanity. Shaker doors are versatile and familiar. Slab fronts create a cleaner, more contemporary profile. Raised-panel doors bring traditional depth. The right choice depends on the home’s architecture, the adjacent rooms, and the mood you want to create.

Set a Clear Budget With Room for the Right Priorities

Custom does not mean every feature must be premium. It means the vanity is designed around your priorities. The investment can vary based on size, wood species, finish complexity, interior accessories, countertop selection, hardware, and whether plumbing or electrical work is involved.

Be honest about what matters most. If storage is the daily pain point, invest in drawer construction and smart interior organization. If the bathroom is a showpiece primary suite, a more detailed finish or furniture-style design may be worth the added cost. If you are improving a secondary bath before selling, durable, well-proportioned cabinetry with simpler details may offer the right balance.

A clear estimate should distinguish cabinetry, countertops, installation, and any related remodeling work. That clarity helps prevent the common renovation problem of discovering essential costs after decisions have already been made. A good cabinetry partner will explain options without pressure and help you understand where a change adds meaningful value versus where it simply adds expense.

Work With a Cabinetry Partner Who Plans the Details

The difference between a vanity that merely fits and one that feels made for your home is often found in the planning. Door and drawer clearances, filler pieces, countertop overhang, sink placement, lighting, wall conditions, and installation sequencing all deserve attention before construction begins.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, that planning is part of creating a bathroom renovation with fewer surprises. A thoughtful design conversation helps align the cabinetry with your timeline, investment level, and the way your family lives. Whether the right solution is fully custom solid wood cabinetry or a more budget-conscious cabinet option, the finished room should feel considered, dependable, and personal.

The right vanity becomes part of the rhythm of home life. Choose one that gives you a place for the everyday clutter, a surface you are proud to see each morning, and craftsmanship you can enjoy long after the renovation is finished.

title: 12 Best Pantry Cabinet Ideas for a Better Kitchen
excerpt: Explore the best pantry cabinet ideas for a kitchen that stays organized, looks refined, and supports easier family meals, hosting, and Nashville homes.
content:
A pantry should not feel like the place where groceries disappear. When shelves are too deep, storage is too limited, or the layout does not match the way your family cooks, even a beautiful kitchen can feel frustrating. The best pantry cabinet ideas create a home for everyday essentials while making meal prep, school mornings, and weekend hosting feel noticeably easier.

For homeowners in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, and Belle Meade, a pantry upgrade is often one of the most practical ways to make a kitchen work harder without sacrificing the refined look they want. The right answer depends on your room, budget, and habits, but thoughtful cabinetry can turn a crowded storage zone into one of the most satisfying parts of the kitchen.

Best Pantry Cabinet Ideas That Solve Everyday Clutter

1. Build a tall pull-out pantry beside the refrigerator

A tall pull-out pantry is an excellent solution for narrow spaces that would otherwise become filler. Instead of reaching into a deep cabinet and losing track of what is behind the cereal boxes, the entire pantry glides forward on heavy-duty hardware. Everything remains visible from both sides.

This option works especially well near the refrigerator, where snacks, breakfast items, and lunch supplies are naturally within reach. It is not always the best choice for very heavy bulk storage, however. A full-height pull-out needs quality slides and a well-built cabinet box to stay smooth and dependable over time.

2. Choose deep drawers for lower pantry storage

Lower shelves are where canned goods, bags of flour, small appliances, and heavier items tend to become a mess. Deep pantry drawers bring the contents out to you, so there is no kneeling on the floor to search behind a row of containers.

Drawers can be fitted with dividers for snacks, baking supplies, pet food, or produce. For households that cook frequently, this is one of the most meaningful upgrades because it improves visibility without requiring a larger pantry footprint.

3. Add adjustable shelves for flexibility

Fixed shelves can look clean on day one, then become limiting as your storage needs change. Adjustable shelving gives a pantry cabinet a longer useful life. You can create tall space for small appliances and oversized cereal boxes, then move shelves later when your needs shift.

The key is not simply adding more shelves. Shelves that are too close together make the pantry feel crowded and waste valuable vertical space. A thoughtful design balances everyday items with a few taller zones for serving trays, countertop appliances, or party supplies.

4. Create a dedicated baking cabinet

Baking is easier when flour, sugar, mixing bowls, parchment paper, and measuring tools live together. A dedicated baking pantry cabinet can include pull-out shelves, drawer dividers, vertical storage for baking sheets, and space for a stand mixer.

For some homeowners, a lift shelf for a heavy mixer is worth considering. It keeps the appliance accessible without leaving it on the counter. It does add cost and requires careful planning, so it makes the most sense when baking is a regular part of your family routine.

5. Use vertical dividers for trays and cutting boards

Cookie sheets, cooling racks, cutting boards, and serving platters are awkward on standard horizontal shelves. Vertical dividers keep these items upright, easy to grab, and protected from constant stacking and unstacking.

This small detail has an outsized effect on daily use. A narrow cabinet near the oven or prep area is often the ideal location, since the items are stored where they are used. It also prevents a large pantry from becoming the catchall for every flat kitchen item.

6. Include a countertop appliance garage

A pantry cabinet with a built-in counter can house the coffee maker, toaster, blender, or other daily appliances. Doors can close when guests arrive, leaving the main kitchen counters clear and calm.

This idea is particularly valuable in open-concept homes, where kitchen clutter is visible from the living and dining areas. Good planning matters here. Appliances need adequate depth, accessible outlets, and enough clearance for safe use. A closed cabinet is not a place to run heat-producing appliances unless the design accounts for ventilation and manufacturer guidance.

7. Design a walk-in pantry with cabinetry, not just wire shelves

Walk-in pantries offer generous storage, but they can still feel unfinished when they rely only on basic wire shelving. Cabinetry, wood shelves, drawers, and a tailored arrangement give the space a more intentional look while improving organization.

Consider shallow shelves around the perimeter so food remains visible, with deeper lower cabinets for bulky items. A small counter can provide a landing place for grocery unloading or serving prep. Even a compact walk-in pantry can feel elevated when its storage is planned around what your household actually buys.

8. Add a pantry cabinet wall for a built-in look

A wall of pantry cabinets can provide the storage of a walk-in pantry without giving up a separate room. Full-height cabinets create a tailored, furniture-like appearance and can be designed to blend beautifully with the rest of the kitchen.

This approach is especially useful during a kitchen renovation when the existing pantry is undersized or poorly placed. The trade-off is that tall cabinetry can make a smaller kitchen feel heavier if every cabinet is dark or visually solid. Mixing in glass-front uppers, lighter finishes, or an open section can keep the wall from feeling imposing.

Pantry Cabinet Details Worth Planning Early

9. Make a place for groceries before they come home

A landing zone near the garage entry, refrigerator, or kitchen island can make grocery day much less chaotic. If your family carries groceries in through a mudroom, a pantry cabinet near that path may be more useful than a pantry tucked across the kitchen.

Location is often more important than size. The most beautiful pantry will still frustrate you if every grocery trip requires crossing the room several times to put food away.

10. Use door storage carefully

Door-mounted racks are useful for spices, wraps, condiments, and other slim items. They can free up shelf space and keep frequently used products at eye level.

Still, door storage has limits. Overloading it can affect how a door hangs and closes, particularly on a tall cabinet. It is best used for lighter items, with sturdy hinges and a cabinet built to handle the added movement.

11. Plan for pet food and household supplies

A family pantry rarely holds food alone. Many homeowners also need room for pet supplies, water bottles, paper goods, lunchboxes, and cleaning products. Giving these categories a defined place prevents them from taking over the kitchen cabinets.

A low pull-out drawer works well for pet food, while a tall utility cabinet can hold brooms, a vacuum, or paper towel rolls. If cleaning products are included, keep them separate from food and consider a lockable area when young children are in the home.

12. Choose materials and finishes that support real life

Pantry cabinetry should feel cohesive with the kitchen, but it does not need to be identical. A painted pantry can complement stained wood kitchen cabinets, or an interior finished in a warm wood tone can add a welcome custom touch behind painted doors.

Solid wood construction, durable drawer boxes, dependable hinges, and properly installed hardware matter more here than trendy accessories. Pantry cabinets are opened constantly and often carry significant weight. Quality craftsmanship is what keeps the space operating beautifully after the novelty of a remodel has passed.

Start With Your Household, Not a Pinterest Board

Before selecting a layout, take a quick inventory of how you use your kitchen for one week. Notice what stays on the counter, what gets lost in the back of cabinets, and which items your family reaches for every day. Those observations will tell you whether you need more drawers, a better appliance zone, a tall cabinet wall, or a walk-in pantry redesign.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, the goal is not to sell every possible feature. It is to create cabinetry that fits your home, your routines, and your budget with a clear plan from the start. A well-designed pantry does more than hold groceries. It gives your kitchen a quieter rhythm, leaving more room to enjoy the meals and people that bring everyone there.

Storage Built for Your Space

Pantries, vanities, mudroom lockers, and window seats: we design and build custom built-ins for Nashville homes, scribed to fit walls that are rarely square. Pair them with custom cabinetry or custom millwork and trim for a consistent look room to room.

title: How to Budget a Bathroom Renovation Without Surprises
excerpt: Learn how to budget a bathroom renovation with a clear plan for priorities, materials, labor, and contingencies so your Nashville project stays on track.
content:
A bathroom renovation can look straightforward from the doorway: new tile, a better vanity, fresh fixtures. Then the walls open, a plumbing line needs to move, or the vanity you love requires a different layout. Knowing how to budget a bathroom renovation before design decisions start is what turns that uncertainty into a project you can enjoy planning.

For homeowners in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, and Belle Meade, the goal is rarely to create a bathroom that simply looks updated. It is to create a space that works better on busy mornings, feels more restful at the end of the day, and adds lasting value to the home. A thoughtful budget gives you room to pursue those goals without making expensive choices under pressure.

Start With the Life You Want the Bathroom to Support

Before assigning dollars to materials, decide what must change. A guest bath used occasionally has different needs than a primary bath shared by two people every morning. Is storage the daily frustration? Is the shower too small, the lighting unflattering, or the existing layout inefficient? The answer should shape every line of the budget.

Write down your non-negotiables, your strong preferences, and the features that would be nice if the budget allows. Keep the first category short. For example, a walk-in shower, more drawer storage, and improved ventilation may matter more than a specialty wall finish or a freestanding tub.

This is also the moment to decide whether the layout stays in place. Keeping the toilet, shower, and vanity plumbing where they are can protect a significant portion of the budget. Moving them may be worthwhile when the current room truly fails your household, but it adds labor, time, permitting considerations, and the possibility of discoveries behind the walls.

How to Budget a Bathroom Renovation by Scope

A reliable bathroom budget begins with scope, not a single number pulled from a renovation show or a neighbor’s project. Two bathrooms of the same size can have dramatically different costs based on layout changes, material choices, the condition of the home, and the level of craftsmanship involved.

A cosmetic refresh might include paint, lighting, a new vanity, countertop, faucet, mirror, and flooring. A full renovation can involve demolition, new plumbing and electrical work, waterproofing, tile installation, cabinetry, countertops, glass, ventilation, and finish work. A primary suite expansion is a different level again, often involving structural changes and a more involved design process.

Ask for estimates that clearly separate the major parts of the work. You should be able to see what is included for demolition, labor, materials, cabinetry or vanity work, plumbing, electrical, tile, fixtures, and project management. Clear allowances are equally important. If an estimate includes an allowance for tile or plumbing fixtures, know the amount before you begin shopping. A beautiful selection that exceeds that allowance is not necessarily wrong, but it should be a conscious choice.

Build the Budget Around the Work That Cannot Be Seen

Homeowners naturally focus on the finishes they will see every day. Those choices matter, but the less visible work is where a bathroom earns its longevity. Waterproofing behind a shower, proper substrate preparation, dependable plumbing connections, safe electrical work, and effective ventilation should never be treated as optional upgrades.

A lower-priced quote may not include the same preparation, materials, or installation standards as a more detailed proposal. Compare scope line by line rather than comparing a final number alone. If one proposal seems substantially lower, ask what is excluded, what assumptions were made, and how change orders are handled.

Cabinetry is a good example of a decision with real budget range. A well-chosen stock or RTA vanity can be a practical fit for a secondary bath or a tighter renovation budget. For a primary bath with unusual dimensions, demanding storage needs, or a specific architectural look, custom cabinetry can make far better use of the room. The right answer depends on how you live, not on choosing the most expensive option by default.

Set Aside a Contingency Before You Commit

Every renovation needs a contingency fund. In an older Middle Tennessee home, opening walls can reveal water damage, outdated wiring, uneven framing, or plumbing that needs attention before new finishes go in. None of these are the fun parts of a renovation, but addressing them correctly protects the investment you are making.

Plan for a contingency of roughly 10% to 20% of the construction budget. The more extensive the demolition, layout changes, or age-related unknowns, the more prudent it is to stay toward the higher end. This is not an invitation to spend freely. It is a reserve that keeps an unexpected repair from forcing rushed compromises elsewhere.

Treat design upgrades separately from contingency. If you decide halfway through that you want heated floors or a different stone countertop, that is a scope change. A contingency is for legitimate unknown conditions, not for additions that were not part of the original plan. Keeping those categories separate makes conversations about cost straightforward and fair.

Make High-Impact Selections in the Right Order

Some decisions influence many others. Confirm the layout first, then select cabinetry or the vanity, shower dimensions, tile direction, and countertop. Fixtures, lighting, mirrors, hardware, and paint should follow. This sequence prevents the common problem of falling in love with an item that does not fit the design, the plumbing plan, or the budget.

Spend intentionally where you interact with the room most. In many bathrooms, that means a durable vanity with useful storage, a properly built shower, comfortable lighting, and hardware that feels substantial in the hand. These are daily-use elements, not background details.

Then look for smart places to simplify. A classic porcelain tile can create a polished look without the cost of a rare imported stone. Using a standard vanity width may reduce both cabinetry and countertop costs. Keeping a beautiful but simple tile pattern can limit installation labor while still giving the room character. Thoughtful restraint often produces a more timeless result than trying to make every surface a statement.

Protect Your Budget From Late Changes

The most expensive decisions are often the ones made after work has started. A clear plan, signed selections, and confirmed measurements reduce costly changes and delays. Before demolition, make sure you understand the location of every fixture, the vanity size, tile choices, shower glass approach, lighting placement, and who is responsible for supplying each item.

Lead times deserve attention, too. A vanity, specialty tile, custom glass panel, or plumbing fixture that arrives late can affect the schedule and may create storage or labor complications. Ordering key items early is not just about convenience. It helps preserve the timeline and prevents last-minute substitutions that do not meet your expectations.

It also helps to create a decision calendar. Choose materials before the point at which the installer needs them, rather than waiting until the room is already open. A professional remodeling partner should guide this process, explain decisions in plain language, and flag budget impacts before they become surprises.

Ask Questions That Create Real Pricing Clarity

A trustworthy estimate should leave you feeling informed, not pressured. Before selecting a contractor, ask how the project scope is documented, how allowances work, what triggers a change order, and how unexpected conditions are communicated. Ask whether permits are needed for the planned work and whether that process is included in the proposal.

You should also discuss the payment schedule, projected timeline, site protection, and cleanup expectations. Remodeling is disruptive even when it is well managed. Knowing how your home will be treated during construction provides just as much peace of mind as knowing the tile color.

Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom approaches renovation planning with the belief that premium craftsmanship and practical budgeting belong in the same conversation. Whether your project calls for a tailored vanity solution or a more budget-conscious approach, the best plan is one that is clearly scoped, thoughtfully designed, and built for the way your family lives.

A bathroom budget is not a limit on what your home can become. It is the plan that lets you choose with confidence, protect what matters most, and look forward to a finished space that feels right every time you walk in.

Storage Built for Your Space

Pantries, vanities, mudroom lockers, and window seats: we design and build custom built-ins for Nashville homes, scribed to fit walls that are rarely square. Pair them with custom cabinetry or custom millwork and trim for a consistent look room to room.
