title: Inset vs Frameless Cabinets: Which Fits Your Kitchen?
excerpt: Compare inset vs frameless cabinets for style, storage, cost, and upkeep. Choose the right cabinet construction for your Nashville kitchen remodel plans.
content:
A cabinet door can change the entire feeling of a kitchen. When homeowners compare inset vs frameless cabinets, they are usually deciding between two very different looks: the tailored, furniture-like precision of inset cabinetry and the clean, expansive lines of frameless construction. Both can be beautiful, durable choices. The right one depends on how you want your kitchen to look, how you use it every day, and where you want to invest your remodeling budget.

For a Nashville kitchen renovation, this choice deserves more than a quick decision based on a showroom photo. Cabinet construction affects storage space, hardware, installation precision, future adjustments, and the overall character of the room.

What Are Inset Cabinets?

Inset cabinets have doors and drawer fronts that sit inside the cabinet frame rather than resting over it. When closed, the fronts sit flush with the face frame, creating an even, intentional grid across the cabinetry. Small, consistent gaps around each door and drawer are part of the design.

This construction has a classic, built-in appearance that feels at home in traditional, transitional, historic, and high-end custom kitchens. It is especially appealing to homeowners who want cabinetry to resemble fine furniture or architectural millwork rather than a standard kitchen installation.

Because each door must fit precisely within its opening, inset cabinetry requires careful fabrication and skilled installation. A cabinet that is even slightly out of square, or a door that is not adjusted correctly, can make the reveals look uneven. That precision is not a drawback when the work is done well. It is exactly what gives inset cabinets their polished, custom appearance.

Why homeowners choose inset cabinetry

The biggest reason is visual character. Inset doors create shadow lines that make painted finishes, natural wood grain, decorative hinges, and detailed door profiles feel more deliberate. They work beautifully with shaker doors, beaded inset styles, flat-panel designs, and more traditional raised-panel doors.

Inset cabinets also offer a strong sense of permanence. In a Brentwood, Franklin, or Belle Meade home where the kitchen connects to formal living spaces or architectural trim, the cabinetry can feel like a natural extension of the home rather than a separate component.

There are practical considerations, though. Since the doors fit inside the openings, inset construction gives up a small amount of accessible opening width compared with overlay doors. It can also cost more due to the labor, materials, and adjustment time involved. For homeowners who value refined details and long-term visual impact, that investment can be worthwhile.

What Are Frameless Cabinets?

Frameless cabinets, often called European-style cabinets, do not use a traditional face frame on the front of the cabinet box. Instead, doors and drawer fronts attach directly to the cabinet sides. Most frameless kitchens use full-overlay doors, meaning the fronts cover much of the cabinet box edge when closed.

The result is a streamlined, modern look with broad door and drawer faces and narrow visible gaps. Frameless cabinetry is popular in contemporary kitchens, but it is not limited to sleek white slab doors. A well-designed frameless cabinet package can also support warm wood finishes, shaker doors, and transitional styling.

Because there is no face frame taking up room at the opening, frameless cabinets often provide slightly more usable interior access. That can be helpful with wide drawers, pull-out storage, tray dividers, pantry systems, and other features designed around real family routines.

Why homeowners choose frameless cabinetry

Frameless cabinets are often the practical choice for homeowners who want a clean look, efficient storage, and a budget that leaves room for other priorities, such as countertops, lighting, flooring, or appliances. They are commonly available in both semi-custom and ready-to-assemble cabinet lines, which can make them a strong option for a faster, value-conscious remodel.

The style is less about being cold or ultra-modern than many people assume. Pair frameless cabinets with a warm white finish, natural oak accents, aged brass hardware, or a softly veined stone countertop, and the kitchen can feel inviting and timeless.

Quality still matters. Frameless boxes rely on solid construction, dependable joinery, and properly installed hardware. A well-built frameless cabinet should feel sturdy, align cleanly, and support drawers and doors that operate smoothly for years.

Inset vs Frameless Cabinets: The Differences That Matter

The visual difference is immediate. Inset cabinetry highlights the cabinet frame and the craftsmanship of each individual opening. Frameless cabinetry minimizes visible structure, allowing the door and drawer fronts to read as larger, cleaner surfaces.

Storage is another meaningful distinction. Frameless cabinetry generally offers more accessible opening space because there is no face frame along the front edge. The difference is modest in a single cabinet, but it can be valuable in a compact kitchen or in a layout where every inch of drawer and pantry storage matters.

Cost often separates the two choices as well. Inset cabinets usually require a higher investment because the tolerances are tighter and installation takes more time. Frameless cabinets can range widely in price, from budget-conscious stock options to high-quality custom construction, but they are often the more economical path to a polished kitchen.

Maintenance deserves an honest look. Both styles need normal cleaning and occasional hinge adjustments. Inset doors have narrow reveals that need to stay consistent, so seasonal movement in wood and routine settling can make expert adjustment more important over time. Middle Tennessee humidity changes are one reason material selection, finishing, and installation accuracy should never be treated as afterthoughts.

A Quick Note About Cabinet Terminology

“Inset” and “frameless” are not perfectly opposite terms. Inset describes how the door sits in relation to the cabinet opening. Frameless describes the construction of the cabinet box. Traditional face-frame cabinets can also use full-overlay or partial-overlay doors.

Still, in most kitchen planning conversations, homeowners are comparing the inset look with the full-overlay frameless look. A good cabinet designer should clarify the construction, door style, material, and hardware together so there are no surprises once the project is underway.

Which Style Fits Your Home and Budget?

Choose inset cabinets when you are drawn to tailored craftsmanship, balanced proportions, and a kitchen that feels deeply connected to the architecture of your home. They are a natural fit for custom renovations where details such as crown molding, custom hoods, paneled appliances, and furniture-style islands are part of the vision.

Choose frameless cabinets when you want maximum storage access, simple contemporary lines, and more flexibility in your budget. They can be an excellent choice for a family kitchen that needs hardworking drawers, organized pantry storage, and a fresh look without overcomplicating the project.

There is no rule that says a traditional home requires inset cabinetry or that a modern home must be frameless. A transitional kitchen may look best with full-overlay shaker doors, while a contemporary home may gain warmth and distinction from carefully designed inset white oak cabinetry. The cabinet style should support the way the room feels as a whole.

Do Not Choose From a Door Sample Alone

A cabinet sample can show color and door profile, but it cannot tell you how the kitchen will function. Before making a decision, consider the full plan: drawer sizes, appliance locations, traffic flow, storage needs, countertop overhangs, lighting, and the visual relationship between cabinetry and surrounding trim.

This is also where clear planning protects your budget. A design that looks simple can become expensive if it calls for extensive fillers, unusual modifications, complex appliance panels, or highly detailed millwork. On the other hand, the right cabinet line and construction method can create a high-end result while keeping the scope aligned with your priorities.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, the goal is not to push one cabinet style over another. It is to help homeowners make confident choices, understand the trade-offs before work begins, and create a kitchen that feels right for the home and the people who gather there.

The best cabinet choice is the one you will still appreciate on an ordinary Tuesday morning: doors that close well, drawers that hold what you need, finishes that make the room feel like yours, and craftsmanship that lets you enjoy your kitchen without second-guessing the decision.

title: 12 Best Bathroom Vanity Storage Ideas for Real Life
excerpt: Explore the best bathroom vanity storage ideas for a calmer, more functional bath, with smart cabinetry solutions tailored to your family’s daily routine.
content:
A beautiful bathroom can still feel frustrating when the counter is crowded with skincare, drawers become a jumble, and towels have nowhere useful to land. The best bathroom vanity storage ideas do more than hide clutter. They create an easier morning routine, protect the finishes you invested in, and make a shared bathroom feel calm instead of cramped.

For homeowners in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, and throughout Middle Tennessee, the right answer is rarely one oversized cabinet. It is a vanity designed around how your household actually gets ready, stores supplies, and uses the room day after day.

Start With What Needs a Home

Before selecting door styles or countertop colors, take inventory of what lives in the bathroom now. Daily-use items need quick access. Backup toiletries, extra paper goods, cleaning supplies, and hair tools need their own controlled space. A vanity that looks generous on a floor plan can still fall short if its interior is divided poorly.

Think about who uses the bath. A primary bathroom may need separate grooming zones for two adults. A hall bath may need durable storage for children, guests, and linen overflow. A powder room usually benefits from a smaller, cleaner arrangement that keeps essentials out of sight without overwhelming the room.

12 Best Bathroom Vanity Storage Ideas

1. Deep Drawers Instead of Open Cabinets

Deep drawers are among the most useful upgrades in a bathroom vanity. They bring the contents forward, so you are not kneeling on the floor and reaching behind plumbing to find a bottle that has disappeared into the back of the cabinet.

Use them for towels, styling tools, larger skincare bottles, and backstock supplies. Full-extension drawer hardware makes a meaningful difference here, particularly in a busy family bathroom. The trade-off is that drawers need careful planning around the sink and plumbing, which is where custom cabinetry can make every inch work harder.

2. A Drawer Within a Drawer

Shallow interior drawers keep small items from getting lost in a larger drawer. This is an excellent solution for cosmetics, razors, toothbrush accessories, medication, and everyday grooming tools.

The top tray can hold frequently used items, while the deeper space beneath handles bulkier supplies. It delivers a tidy, tailored look without asking you to reorganize every week.

3. U-Shaped Drawers Around the Sink

The area beneath a sink is often treated as unusable space. It does not have to be. U-shaped drawers are built to work around drain pipes, creating usable storage on both sides and in front of the plumbing.

This option is especially valuable in a smaller vanity, where every available inch matters. It costs more than a basic open cabinet, but homeowners often find the added organization well worth it in a primary bath or compact guest bath.

4. Vertical Pullouts for Hair Tools

Curling irons, flat irons, hair dryers, brushes, and cords quickly take over a vanity drawer. A narrow vertical pullout gives these tools a dedicated home and keeps them separated from makeup and toiletries.

For the best result, include heat-resistant holders and allow the tool to cool fully before storing it. A custom pullout can be sized to the tools you already own instead of forcing your routine to fit a standard cabinet box.

5. Built-In Electrical Outlets

An outlet inside a drawer or cabinet makes a bathroom feel immediately more considered. It allows electric toothbrushes, shavers, and styling tools to charge out of view, leaving the countertop cleaner and easier to wipe down.

Electrical storage requires proper planning and installation. It also works best when paired with a drawer or cabinet designed to manage cords safely rather than pinching or tangling them.

6. Divided Top Drawers

The top drawer should earn its place. Instead of one wide, undefined space, use adjustable dividers to create clear zones for the items you reach for each morning.

A simple division between dental care, skincare, cosmetics, and grooming supplies can eliminate most counter clutter. Choose dividers that are easy to remove and clean, especially in bathrooms used by children or guests.

7. Tall Linen Storage Beside the Vanity

If your bathroom layout allows it, a tall linen cabinet beside the vanity can solve several storage problems at once. It provides a place for folded towels, washcloths, extra toiletries, and less attractive necessities without filling every vanity drawer.

A tall cabinet also adds visual balance to a long vanity wall. In a smaller room, consider a shallower cabinet depth so it adds storage without narrowing the walkway.

8. Open Shelves for Everyday Towels

Open shelving is not right for every household, but it can be a warm, practical choice when used with intention. A lower shelf beneath the vanity keeps neatly folded towels within easy reach and makes the room feel less heavy than a full wall of closed cabinetry.

The key is restraint. Open storage works best for attractive, frequently used items. Reserve closed cabinets and drawers for personal products, cleaning supplies, and the ordinary visual clutter of real life.

9. Pullout Hampers

A built-in hamper keeps damp towels and laundry from landing on the floor or collecting in a bedroom corner. It is particularly helpful in a primary suite, where laundry tends to accumulate at the end of a long day.

Ventilation matters. A removable liner makes the hamper easier to clean, while a cabinet location away from splash zones helps protect the surrounding materials.

10. Toe-Kick Drawers

The space beneath a vanity can become shallow, hidden storage with toe-kick drawers. These are well suited to spare washcloths, cleaning cloths, travel toiletries, or other low-profile items you do not need every day.

Toe-kick drawers are a smart custom feature, though they are not essential in every project. They provide the most value when the bathroom is short on square footage and the vanity is already being built specifically for the room.

11. A Dedicated Charging and Grooming Station

For couples sharing a bathroom, separate grooming storage can make mornings noticeably smoother. One drawer might hold a charging station and electric grooming tools, while another is organized for cosmetics, skincare, or hair accessories.

This approach is less about having more cabinetry and more about preventing one person’s routine from taking over the entire vanity. Clear zones reduce friction, especially when two people are getting ready at the same time.

12. Make the Medicine Cabinet Work Harder

A recessed medicine cabinet can add useful storage without taking up vanity space. Modern options can be wider, taller, and more refined than the shallow mirrored boxes many homeowners remember.

Use it for small, lightweight items that need to stay accessible. If the wall cavity or electrical layout prevents a recessed cabinet, a surface-mounted design may still be worthwhile, but it should be selected carefully so it feels intentional within the room’s proportions.

Choose Storage That Fits the Vanity Style

Storage should support the look of the bathroom, not compete with it. A clean-lined contemporary vanity may benefit from wide drawers with discreet integrated pulls. A more traditional bathroom may call for framed cabinetry, furniture-style legs, and a tall linen cabinet that feels like part of the architecture.

Material selection matters, too. Bathrooms experience moisture, temperature changes, and frequent cleaning. Well-built solid wood cabinetry, quality finishes, and reliable drawer hardware protect your investment over time. Stock cabinet options can be a sensible choice for a budget-conscious remodel, while fully custom cabinetry gives you more control over dimensions, interior storage, and finish details.

Plan Storage Before Construction Begins

The most expensive bathroom storage mistake is trying to add it after the vanity has been ordered or installed. Plumbing locations, outlet placement, sink size, door swings, and walkway clearances all influence what can realistically fit.

During the design stage, bring measurements of baskets, hair tools, countertop appliances, and the products you use regularly. Consider what may change, too. A bathroom designed for a growing family needs different storage than one designed for occasional guests or aging in place.

A clear plan also keeps the remodeling process more predictable. When the cabinet layout, materials, and interior features are decided early, there are fewer surprises once work begins. Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom helps homeowners make those decisions with a practical eye for craftsmanship, budget, and daily use.

The right vanity storage should make your bathroom feel easier to live in from the first morning you use it. Choose the features that solve your actual frustrations, leave room for the routines ahead, and let the finished space feel as peaceful as it looks.

Storage Built for Your Space

title: 10 Frameless Kitchen Cabinet Ideas That Work
excerpt: See frameless kitchen cabinet ideas that bring cleaner lines, smarter storage, and a tailored fit to your Nashville-area kitchen renovation and detail.
content:
A kitchen can have beautiful finishes and still feel dated if its cabinetry is crowded by wide face frames, uneven reveals, and wasted interior space. The best frameless kitchen cabinet ideas solve those quiet frustrations with clean lines, full-access storage, and a more tailored appearance. For homeowners in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, and Belle Meade, this cabinet style is often the starting point for a kitchen that feels current without feeling cold.

Frameless cabinetry is not simply a modern look. It is a construction method that can make everyday cooking, hosting, and organizing easier. The right design depends on your home’s architecture, how your family uses the room, and where you want to invest. Here are ideas worth considering before you select doors, finishes, and hardware.

What Makes Frameless Cabinets Different?

Traditional framed cabinets have a solid wood face frame across the front of the box. Frameless cabinets, sometimes called European-style cabinets, omit that front frame. Doors and drawer fronts mount directly to the cabinet box, leaving a slimmer gap between them.

That construction creates a more continuous wall of cabinetry and gives you greater access to the interior. A few extra inches of usable width in a base cabinet may not sound significant on paper, but it matters when you are reaching for sheet pans, storing cookware, or fitting pullout organizers.

The trade-off is that precision matters more. Frameless cabinets rely on accurately built boxes, quality hardware, and careful installation to maintain even lines. A well-designed project should not ask you to choose between refined appearance and dependable construction. It should deliver both.

1. Use Full-Overlay Doors for a Clean, Tailored Front

Full-overlay doors are the natural partner for frameless construction. They cover most of the cabinet box edge, producing narrow, consistent reveals between each door and drawer. The result is orderly and polished, whether you prefer a warm transitional kitchen or a crisp contemporary one.

For a softer look in a traditional Nashville home, choose a slim shaker door with a painted finish. For a more architectural result, use a flat-panel door in white oak, walnut, or a matte painted color. The frameless construction keeps either choice from looking visually heavy.

2. Build a Two-Tone Kitchen With a Grounded Island

Frameless cabinets make two-tone schemes feel intentional because the cabinet lines remain clean and uninterrupted. A common approach is light perimeter cabinets with a deeper island – navy, charcoal, soft black, or a rich stained wood all work well.

This is also a practical way to add warmth to a large kitchen. Lighter upper cabinets can keep the room open, while darker or wood-toned base cabinets give the space a sense of permanence. The key is restraint. Choose one dominant cabinet finish and one supporting finish, then repeat an accent through stools, lighting, or hardware.

3. Choose Wood Grain for Warm Modern Character

Not every frameless kitchen needs a high-gloss white finish. Rift-cut white oak, walnut, and other carefully selected wood veneers or solid wood door options can bring depth and natural character to the clean geometry of frameless cabinetry.

Vertical grain on tall pantry cabinets can make ceilings feel higher. Horizontal grain on a long run of base cabinets can emphasize the width of the room. In a home with existing beams, hardwood floors, or traditional millwork, wood cabinetry can bridge old and new instead of competing with either.

Wood does require thoughtful finish selection. A busy household may benefit from a durable, low-sheen finish that is forgiving around fingerprints and daily wear. Your cabinet finish should support real life, not create another surface to worry about.

4. Replace Lower Doors With Deep, Organized Drawers

One of the smartest frameless kitchen cabinet ideas has little to do with style: favor drawers over standard lower doors wherever possible. Deep drawers bring pots, small appliances, dishes, and pantry staples forward instead of sending you searching at the back of a cabinet.

A drawer base can include shallow top drawers for utensils or linens and deeper drawers below for cookware. Add dividers for plates, adjustable pegs for bowls, or a dedicated insert for food containers. These details make the kitchen easier to reset after dinner and easier for everyone in the family to use.

Drawers can cost more than a simple door-and-shelf cabinet, so prioritize them in the areas that will make the greatest difference: next to the range, around the cleanup zone, and in your most-used prep area.

5. Make the Pantry Work Harder

A tall frameless pantry cabinet can look calm from the outside while doing serious work inside. Full-height doors create a clean elevation, especially when they align with surrounding wall cabinets. Behind them, rollout trays, adjustable shelves, spice storage, and interior drawers can turn a cluttered pantry into a functional zone.

For families who buy in bulk, consider a combination of deep shelves for larger items and shallower pullouts for cans and snacks. For a smaller kitchen, a well-planned pantry cabinet may eliminate the need for a separate pantry room. It depends on the layout, but the goal is the same: make food storage visible, reachable, and easy to maintain.

6. Create an Appliance Wall That Looks Like Furniture

Refrigerators, wall ovens, coffee stations, and pantry storage can quickly make a kitchen feel fragmented. Frameless cabinetry helps turn those components into one composed appliance wall.

Panel-ready refrigeration, tall pantry cabinets, and integrated appliance garages can reduce visual clutter while preserving convenience. A coffee station behind pocket doors is especially useful for homeowners who want countertop access in the morning and a cleaner room when guests arrive.

Be realistic about clearances and ventilation requirements before committing to a built-in look. Custom cabinetry is valuable here because it can be designed around the actual appliance specifications rather than forcing an expensive appliance into a cabinet plan that was not made for it.

7. Extend Cabinets to the Ceiling

The gap above standard upper cabinets tends to collect dust and visually shortens the room. Taking frameless cabinetry to the ceiling creates a more finished appearance and adds valuable storage for serving pieces, seasonal items, or less-used appliances.

In kitchens with tall ceilings, this does not always mean every cabinet should be extra tall. A balanced design may use a main upper cabinet with a smaller top cabinet above it, separated by a subtle horizontal reveal. That approach adds height without making everyday items hard to reach.

8. Let Hardware Support the Design

Frameless cabinets can be made with minimal hardware, integrated pulls, or visible knobs and pulls. Each choice changes the personality of the kitchen.

Long bar pulls reinforce a contemporary look. Small knobs and classic pulls add a more transitional feel. Integrated edge pulls are striking on flat-panel doors, but they may not suit every household if you prefer a more substantial grip. Test hardware in person when possible. It should feel as good in your hand as it looks on the door.

9. Add a Hidden, Purpose-Built Work Zone

A kitchen often needs to accommodate more than cooking. A small desk, charging drawer, pet-feeding station, baking center, or homework landing spot can keep daily clutter from taking over the island.

Frameless cabinet boxes are particularly useful for these custom zones because interior dimensions can be planned around the items you actually own. A charging drawer needs outlets and cord management. A baking cabinet needs vertical storage for pans and enough counter space nearby. The best solution is not the trendiest one – it is the one that quietly improves your routine.

10. Pair the Look With the Right Level of Investment

Frameless does not automatically mean one price point. Some homeowners want fully custom, solid wood cabinetry and millwork tailored to a distinctive home. Others want a budget-conscious stock or RTA cabinet solution with a well-planned layout and professional installation. Both can produce a beautiful kitchen when materials, scope, and expectations are clear from the beginning.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, that conversation starts with how you live in your kitchen, then aligns the design with your budget and priorities. Clear planning helps you decide where custom details will have the most impact and where a simpler solution makes sense.

A frameless kitchen should never feel like a showroom that happens to have a stove. When cabinet lines are precise, storage is planned around your habits, and finishes reflect the character of your home, the result is a room that welcomes people in and makes daily life feel noticeably easier.

title: Semi Custom Cabinetry Options for Your Home
excerpt: Compare semi custom cabinetry options for your Nashville remodel, with practical guidance on style, budget, timing, and custom details that matter most.
content:
A beautiful kitchen should not require choosing between a generic cabinet layout and a fully bespoke price tag. For many Middle Tennessee homeowners, semi custom cabinetry options create the practical middle ground: more choice in style, finish, storage, and sizing than stock cabinets, with a more defined process and investment than fully custom work.

That middle ground matters when you are updating a kitchen in Brentwood, Franklin, Belle Meade, or Nashville. You may love the bones of your home but need a kitchen that holds more, works harder, and feels like it belongs there. The right cabinet choice can bring order to busy mornings, make hosting easier, and give the room a refined look without adding uncertainty to every design decision.

What Semi Custom Cabinetry Actually Means

Semi custom cabinets begin with an established cabinet line rather than being built from scratch for one home. The manufacturer offers a collection of door styles, finishes, cabinet sizes, storage accessories, and construction upgrades. You select from those options, then the cabinetry is specified and installed for your room.

The key difference is flexibility. Stock cabinetry is typically sold in limited widths, heights, colors, and configurations. Fully custom cabinetry can be designed around virtually any dimension, material, profile, or architectural detail. Semi custom sits between the two. It gives you a far wider design palette than stock, while working within a proven manufacturing system.

That does not mean semi custom is automatically the right answer for every project. A kitchen with unusually angled walls, historic trim details, or a need for furniture-style built-ins may benefit from fully custom cabinetry and millwork. On the other hand, if your layout is relatively straightforward and your priority is a polished, personalized kitchen with clearer parameters, semi custom can be an excellent fit.

The Semi Custom Cabinetry Options That Change Daily Life

Homeowners often start with a cabinet color or door style. Those choices matter, but the features behind the doors tend to have the greatest impact after installation. A well-planned semi custom kitchen should support how your family cooks, cleans, gathers, and stores the everyday items that create clutter.

Door Styles and Finishes

Semi custom lines usually offer a meaningful range of door styles, from classic raised-panel doors to clean Shaker profiles and more contemporary slab fronts. This is where you establish the character of the room. A warm painted finish can soften a traditional Nashville home, while natural wood tones bring depth and texture to a newer space.

Finish options are often broader than homeowners expect. Depending on the line, you may be able to choose paint colors, stains, glazes, distressed details, and different sheen levels. Still, this is a point where specifications matter. Two finishes that look similar in a showroom can read very differently in a kitchen with strong afternoon sun or limited natural light. Reviewing samples in your home helps avoid costly surprises.

Cabinet Sizes and Layout Adjustments

Semi custom cabinetry commonly provides more widths, heights, and depths than stock cabinets. That can make a major difference in a room that feels slightly off-balance with standard sizes. You may be able to use a narrower cabinet to eliminate an awkward filler, select taller wall cabinets for extra storage, or choose a deeper base cabinet in a strategic area.

There are limits. If a wall is noticeably out of square, a ceiling slopes sharply, or an opening needs a truly exact fit, custom fillers, panels, or millwork may still be needed. A thoughtful design plan accounts for those details early, rather than treating them as installation-day problems.

Storage Features Worth Considering

Semi custom cabinetry can make organization feel intentional instead of improvised. The most useful upgrades are usually the ones that solve a specific frustration in your current kitchen: a crowded corner, a pantry that loses track of groceries, or a deep cabinet where pots disappear behind one another.

Consider pull-out trash and recycling units near the prep area, deep drawers for cookware, drawer dividers for utensils, rollout trays for pantry cabinets, and vertical storage for baking sheets. Corner solutions can help, too, though the best choice depends on how you use the kitchen. A rotating organizer is useful for some households, while others prefer a blind-corner pullout or simply a well-designed drawer layout nearby.

The goal is not to add every available accessory. It is to invest in the features that remove friction from your everyday routine.

Construction and Material Choices

Cabinet construction deserves more attention than it usually receives. Ask about the cabinet box material, drawer construction, shelving thickness, joinery, hinges, and drawer glides. These details affect how cabinets perform after years of opening, closing, loading, and cleaning.

Some semi custom lines offer upgrades such as plywood construction, solid-wood drawer boxes, soft-close hardware, and stronger shelving. Others may use engineered materials in certain components. Neither approach should be judged by a label alone. What matters is understanding what is included, where upgrades add value, and how the selected cabinet line fits your expectations for durability.

For homeowners comparing semi custom with fully custom solid-wood cabinetry, this is often the deciding conversation. Fully custom work offers exceptional control over materials and construction. Semi custom can deliver a beautiful, dependable kitchen, but it is important to choose it with clear expectations about what is standardized and what can be tailored.

How Semi Custom Cabinetry Affects Your Budget

Semi custom cabinets generally cost more than ready-to-assemble or basic stock cabinets because they offer more sizes, better finish choices, greater design flexibility, and often stronger construction. They typically cost less than fully custom cabinetry because the manufacturing process is already established.

However, cabinet pricing is never just about the cabinet boxes. Door style, finish, construction upgrades, interior accessories, decorative panels, moldings, installation requirements, demolition, electrical changes, countertops, and plumbing can all shape the total remodeling investment.

A simple painted Shaker kitchen with a practical layout may stay comfortably within a moderate budget. A large kitchen with tall cabinets, specialty storage, glass fronts, detailed molding, and a two-tone finish can move much closer to custom pricing. That is not a reason to avoid upgrades. It is a reason to prioritize them intentionally.

A clear proposal should help you see where your money is going and what each selection changes. When the scope is defined before work begins, you can make confident trade-offs instead of being pushed into rushed decisions halfway through the project.

When Semi Custom Is the Best Fit

Semi custom is often a strong choice when you want more than a basic cabinet replacement but do not need every piece built to a one-of-one specification. It works especially well for homeowners who value a curated look, need practical storage improvements, and want a reliable path from design through installation.

It can be a particularly smart solution for a kitchen where the footprint is staying mostly the same. If plumbing, walls, and major openings remain in place, the added sizing and finish choices of semi custom cabinetry may give you the transformation you want without paying for a level of customization the room does not require.

It may be less ideal when architecture is the main challenge. Older homes can have uneven walls and floors, nonstandard openings, and details that need cabinetry to blend precisely with existing millwork. In those cases, a combination approach can be the answer: semi custom cabinets for the main kitchen run, paired with custom panels, a custom hood surround, a built-in banquette, or tailored millwork where it makes the biggest visual difference.

A Better Way to Choose Between Stock, Semi Custom, and Custom

Start with your nonnegotiables, not a cabinet category. Think about the storage problems you want solved, the visual feeling you want in the room, your expected timeline, and the investment range that feels responsible for your household.

Then assess the room itself. Are the walls reasonably straightforward? Do standard and modified cabinet sizes create a balanced layout? Are there areas that demand a precise custom solution? A professional measure and design review can answer these questions before you become attached to a plan that does not fit the space.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, the goal is not to steer every homeowner toward the same product. It is to help you choose a cabinetry path that respects your home, your budget, and the way you actually live. That may mean a budget-conscious stock solution, a carefully specified semi custom kitchen, or fully custom cabinetry and millwork.

Your kitchen does not have to be extravagant to feel personal. Choose the cabinetry that gives you the details you will appreciate every day, then let thoughtful design and precise installation do the rest.

title: Are Shaker Cabinets Still in Style for 2026?
excerpt: Are shaker cabinets still in style? See why this enduring cabinet design works in Nashville kitchens, plus the details that make it feel current today.
content:
A kitchen can have beautiful stone, new appliances, and plenty of square footage, yet still feel dated if the cabinet doors do not suit the home. So, are shaker cabinets still in style? Absolutely. But the Shaker kitchens homeowners are choosing in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, and Belle Meade look more tailored than the all-white, heavily contrasted version that dominated years ago.

The reason is simple: Shaker cabinetry is built on proportion, not decoration. Its recessed center panel and clean frame give a kitchen enough detail to feel intentional without tying it to one short-lived trend. That makes it a strong foundation for a renovation designed to serve your family well now and still feel right years from now.

Why Shaker Cabinets Continue to Work

Shaker doors have a quiet architectural quality. They complement a historic home with traditional millwork, but they can also sit comfortably in a newer home with clean-lined lighting and contemporary hardware. That flexibility matters when a kitchen must work with the rest of the house rather than look like it came from a showroom display.

They are practical, too. The simple profile is easier to clean than deeply carved or highly ornate door styles, and it gives your designer room to make thoughtful choices elsewhere. A beautiful slab backsplash, warm white oak floors, a painted island, or a statement range hood can take the lead without competing with the cabinets.

For homeowners thinking about resale, Shaker cabinets remain a reassuring choice. They are familiar, broadly appealing, and polished without being overly formal. That does not mean every buyer wants the same kitchen. It means the door style gives future owners a versatile backdrop they can live with and personalize.

Are Shaker Cabinets Still in Style? The Details Matter

A Shaker cabinet is not one fixed look. The construction, proportions, finish, hardware, and surrounding materials determine whether it feels classic, current, or stuck in a previous design cycle.

The biggest mistake is treating the door style as the entire design. A narrow rail, generic bright-white paint, busy gray granite, and oversized black pulls can create a kitchen that feels assembled from familiar trend pieces. A well-planned Shaker kitchen feels more considered because its details support the architecture of the home and the way the family uses the room.

Choose proportions that fit the room

Traditional Shaker doors often use narrower frames, while many updated kitchens use a slightly wider, more substantial rail and stile. Neither is automatically better. Narrower profiles can preserve a refined, historic feel, especially in older Nashville homes. Wider frames can give a larger kitchen a grounded, furniture-like presence.

Door proportions should also work with the cabinet scale. Tall pantry doors, wide drawer bases, and large islands need visual balance. Custom cabinetry allows those proportions to be adjusted instead of forcing every opening into a standard size. That is a small design decision with a major effect on the finished room.

Move beyond stark white

White Shaker cabinets are still appropriate in many homes. They brighten a kitchen, reflect natural light, and pair easily with wood, stone, and metal finishes. The difference today is that homeowners are often choosing softer, warmer whites rather than icy tones.

Painted colors are also bringing Shaker cabinetry forward. Mushroom, putty, soft taupe, muted green, deep blue, and warm charcoal all give the door profile a more personal character. A two-tone kitchen can work beautifully as well, such as a warm white perimeter with a stained oak or painted island. The goal is not to chase a color trend. It is to choose a palette that works with your flooring, light exposure, and the finishes already present in your home.

Add warmth with natural materials

The most current Shaker kitchens rarely rely on one finish alone. They balance painted cabinetry with natural wood, handmade-look tile, honed stone, or aged metal. Those layers soften the crisp geometry of the cabinet doors and make the room feel lived in rather than overly polished.

White oak is especially popular because it adds texture without becoming visually heavy. It can be used for an island, open shelving, a hood surround, or selected upper cabinets. In a more traditional home, a richer stained wood may be the better fit. The right choice depends on the home, not on what is most photographed online.

Let hardware support the design

Hardware is often the quickest way to date an otherwise timeless cabinet. Long bar pulls remain useful for large drawers, but they are no longer the only answer. Knobs, smaller pulls, and more sculptural shapes can bring more character to a Shaker kitchen.

Unlacquered brass, bronze, satin nickel, and matte black can all work. Consider the faucet, lighting, and nearby rooms before committing. Matching every metal exactly is not required, but the finishes should feel intentional. A good design plan keeps these decisions connected, so the kitchen feels cohesive instead of crowded with competing choices.

When Shaker May Not Be the Best Choice

Shaker is versatile, not universal. If your home has a distinctly modern architectural style and you prefer an ultra-minimal look, a flat-panel door may be a better fit. Its uninterrupted surface and sharp lines can create the calm, contemporary effect that a framed door cannot fully replicate.

On the other end of the spectrum, an ornate historic home may call for a raised-panel or inset door with more traditional detailing. If the rest of the home includes elaborate crown molding, antique furnishings, and formal rooms, a very simple Shaker profile can feel slightly underdressed unless it is carefully paired with the right millwork and finish.

Budget can also shape the decision. Stock and RTA Shaker cabinets are widely available, which can make them a smart option for a faster, more cost-conscious remodel. However, lower-cost cabinets may offer limited sizes, fewer finish options, and less durable construction. If you have an awkward layout, need better storage, or want cabinetry that aligns precisely with existing architectural features, custom or semi-custom work may provide more value over time.

How to Make a Shaker Kitchen Feel Personal

A timeless door style should never result in a generic kitchen. The best renovations begin with real-life questions: Who cooks? Where do backpacks and mail land? Do you host holidays? Is the kitchen open to the living room? Do you need hidden appliance storage, a baking station, or drawers that make everyday items easier to reach?

Once those answers are clear, cabinetry can be designed around your routines. A custom island may include deep drawers for cookware, a pullout for pet food, and seating that keeps guests close without blocking the cook. A paneled refrigerator and a properly scaled hood can make the room feel more architectural. Interior organizers can reduce countertop clutter and make a busy weekday morning less frustrating.

These choices are why cabinet style should be considered alongside layout and function, not before them. A door sample can look beautiful in isolation, but a kitchen succeeds when every cabinet, finish, and storage solution works together.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, the focus is on helping Middle Tennessee homeowners make those decisions with clear plans, honest options, and craftsmanship that respects both the home and the budget. Whether the right answer is solid-wood custom cabinetry or a well-designed stock cabinet renovation, the process should feel understandable from the first estimate through installation.

A Style That Earns Its Staying Power

Trends will continue to shift toward new colors, metals, and countertop materials. Shaker cabinetry endures because it does not demand attention from every corner of the room. It creates a dependable structure for the choices that make a kitchen yours.

If you are considering a remodel, do not ask only whether a cabinet door is popular this year. Ask whether it suits your home, supports the way your family lives, and gives you a kitchen you will be proud to gather in. When those answers are yes, Shaker cabinets are far more than still in style.

title: Can Stock Cabinets Look Custom? Yes, With Details
excerpt: Can stock cabinets look custom? Smart layout choices, tailored trim, and precise installation can give stock cabinetry a polished built-in look at home.
content:
A kitchen can have beautiful cabinet doors and still look unfinished if the boxes stop short of the ceiling, leave awkward gaps at the walls, or sit on an uneven floor. Those details are why homeowners often ask, can stock cabinets look custom? The answer is yes – when the design, materials, and installation are handled with care.

Stock cabinetry is not the same as fully custom cabinetry. It comes in predetermined sizes, finishes, and configurations. That limitation can be a smart trade-off for a Nashville, Brentwood, or Franklin homeowner who wants a refined kitchen without putting every dollar into made-to-order cabinet boxes. The key is knowing where standard cabinetry works well and where thoughtful customization makes the finished room feel intentional.

Can Stock Cabinets Look Custom in a Real Kitchen?

They can, but cabinets do not look custom simply because they are expensive or painted a popular color. A custom-looking kitchen has proportion, continuity, and clean transitions. The cabinets appear designed for the room rather than selected from a shelf and placed wherever they fit.

That outcome starts with the plan. Before choosing a door style, consider the room’s ceiling height, window placement, traffic flow, appliance dimensions, and the storage your household actually needs. A kitchen that supports weekday breakfasts, holiday cooking, and family gatherings should be arranged around real life, not just a showroom display.

Stock cabinets are especially effective in kitchens with relatively straightforward layouts and standard appliance sizes. They may be less ideal when walls are significantly out of square, ceilings are unusually high, or you need cabinetry shaped around a distinctive architectural feature. In those situations, a blend of stock cabinetry and custom millwork can often provide the right balance of cost and finish quality.

Start With a Layout That Does Not Feel Compromised

The fastest way to make stock cabinets look like stock cabinets is to force them into a layout with visible fillers, narrow gaps, and poorly aligned elements. A good cabinet plan uses standard sizes strategically so the room feels balanced from every angle.

For example, upper cabinets should relate thoughtfully to windows, ranges, and adjacent walls. Base cabinets should create useful work zones rather than leave a drawer bank too close to an appliance handle. An island should have enough clearance for people to pass comfortably, open drawers, and work together without crowding the room.

A professional design plan can also identify small adjustments that make a large visual difference. Shifting an appliance a few inches, changing the width of a drawer base, or selecting a different pantry configuration may eliminate an awkward filler. This is where budget-conscious planning becomes more valuable than simply choosing the lowest-priced cabinet line.

Use fillers as design tools, not leftover space

Fillers are sometimes necessary, especially near walls or when doors need clearance to open. The goal is not to eliminate every filler. It is to size and place them so they look deliberate.

A properly planned filler may be finished with a matching panel, aligned with a stile, or incorporated into a framed end. A random two-inch strip between cabinets, however, draws attention to the fact that the layout was not resolved. Precise measuring and a clear installation plan prevent those last-minute compromises.

Extend Cabinets With Trim and Panels

Custom kitchens often feel elevated because cabinetry is integrated into the architecture. Stock cabinets can create a similar impression with well-chosen trim, finished panels, and careful detailing.

Crown molding is one of the most effective options when it suits the ceiling height and cabinet style. It closes the open space above upper cabinets and creates a stronger visual connection to the room. For a more tailored look, cabinet boxes can be stacked with a smaller upper section or extended with a matching material treatment to reach the ceiling.

Finished end panels matter just as much. The exposed side of an island, refrigerator enclosure, or cabinet run should not look like an unfinished box. A quality panel, furniture-style legs where appropriate, or a recessed base detail can give the cabinetry more presence.

Trim should support the style of the home. A transitional kitchen may benefit from simple crown and clean paneling, while a more traditional Belle Meade home may call for layered molding and more architectural detail. The right choice is not always the most ornate one. It is the one that looks like it belongs.

Choose Door Styles and Finishes With Staying Power

The cabinet door is the most visible surface in the kitchen, but it should not carry the entire design alone. Shaker doors remain popular because they work in many home styles and can look either classic or contemporary depending on the paint color, hardware, and surrounding finishes. Slab doors offer a cleaner, more modern direction. Raised-panel doors can bring warmth and formality to traditional spaces.

For a custom appearance, consistency is more important than chasing a trend. Choose a finish that works with the flooring, wall color, countertop, and natural light in your home. A warm white may feel inviting in one kitchen and yellowed in another. A deep painted island can add contrast, but it needs to relate to the room’s other permanent elements.

Paint quality also affects the final impression. Crisp, durable finishes and clean door alignment make cabinetry feel more substantial. When finish selections are made early, the rest of the design can support them instead of competing for attention.

Let Hardware, Lighting, and Countertops Do Their Part

Hardware is a small investment compared with cabinet replacement, yet it has an outsized impact. Pulls and knobs should feel comfortable in the hand, suit the door style, and be installed consistently. Mixing metals can work beautifully, but only when it is intentional. A kitchen with brushed brass cabinet hardware, for example, may still use another finish at the faucet if the overall palette feels connected.

Lighting is equally important. Under-cabinet lighting makes food prep easier, but it also highlights the backsplash and gives cabinets a finished, welcoming glow in the evening. Layered lighting from recessed fixtures, pendants, and task lighting helps the room feel designed rather than merely equipped.

Countertops and backsplashes complete the visual story. A full-height backsplash behind the range, a waterfall edge on an island, or a carefully selected stone with movement can make standard cabinets feel much more tailored. These choices should be evaluated as a group, not one sample at a time under store lighting.

Installation Is Where the Custom Look Is Won or Lost

Even the best cabinet plan can look disappointing when installation is rushed. Walls and floors in established Middle Tennessee homes are rarely perfectly level, plumb, or square. Cabinet installation requires shimming, scribing, leveling, and detailed adjustment so doors line up, reveals remain even, and countertops have a stable base.

This is also the stage where small details become visible. Cabinet runs should meet walls cleanly. Crown molding should be joined neatly. Appliance panels should align with nearby doors. Drawers should open smoothly, and hardware should sit at consistent heights. Those are the workmanship details homeowners may not notice individually, but they absolutely notice in the overall feeling of the kitchen.

A clear plan also protects the budget. When measurements, materials, and scope are confirmed before work begins, there are fewer surprises once cabinets arrive. It is far easier to make design decisions on paper than to solve them after a countertop template has been scheduled.

Where Stock Cabinets Have Limits

Stock cabinets are a strong option, but they are not the right answer for every project. If you want a curved island, an exact paint match, cabinetry built around irregular stonework, or storage designed for a very specific collection or routine, fully custom work may be worth the investment.

The same is true when a room needs unusual depths, specialized interior organization, or cabinetry that must align exactly with existing millwork. Custom cabinetry gives you control over dimensions, materials, construction, and decorative details. It can make sense for a signature space where nothing short of a precise fit will do.

Many homeowners choose a middle path: stock or RTA cabinets for the main kitchen run, paired with custom panels, a built-in hood surround, a tailored island, or architectural trim. This approach puts the investment where it will be seen and felt most while keeping the project designed for a real budget.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, the goal is not to push every homeowner toward one cabinet category. It is to help you choose the combination that gives your home the right function, finish, and value – with a plan you can feel confident about before the work begins.

A well-designed kitchen should not announce what it cost or where each cabinet came from. It should feel settled, useful, and distinctly yours when the family gathers around the island, the counters are full, and you are proud to invite people in.

title: Bathroom Remodel Planning Guide for Nashville Homes
excerpt: Use this bathroom remodel planning guide to set a realistic budget, refine your layout, and plan a comfortable, lasting Nashville bathroom renovation today.
content:
A bathroom can look dated long before it stops working. The crowded vanity, dim lighting, worn flooring, and lack of storage may be small frustrations on their own, but together they can make every morning feel more difficult than it needs to be. This bathroom remodel planning guide helps Nashville-area homeowners make confident decisions before construction begins, so the finished room feels beautiful, functions well, and fits the way your household actually lives.

Start With How the Bathroom Needs to Work

Before selecting tile or cabinet finishes, identify what is not working in the current space. Is one shared bathroom causing a morning traffic jam? Does a primary bath lack the storage needed for towels, grooming tools, and everyday essentials? Are you planning to age in place, welcoming frequent guests, or simply ready to make a builder-grade room feel more personal?

A clear answer changes the scope of the remodel. A powder room may benefit most from a statement vanity, better lighting, and thoughtful millwork. A primary bathroom may call for a revised layout, a larger shower, two separate vanity zones, or cabinetry designed around daily routines. The best design is not the one with the most features. It is the one that removes the frustrations you notice every day.

Walk through the room at the times you use it most. Notice where people stand, where towels land, what gets left on the counter, and which doors or drawers interfere with one another. These details give your designer and remodeler a much stronger starting point than a collection of inspiration photos alone.

Set a Budget That Matches the Scope

Bathroom remodeling costs can vary widely because the work behind the walls often matters as much as the finishes in front of them. Moving plumbing, correcting water damage, upgrading electrical service, changing a window, or expanding the room all affect the investment. Custom cabinetry, natural stone, specialty tile installation, and premium plumbing fixtures also bring different costs than stock materials.

Start by establishing a comfortable overall investment range, then separate your must-haves from your nice-to-haves. This keeps the project focused when choices begin to multiply. For example, homeowners often decide that a larger shower and durable vanity cabinetry matter more than a freestanding tub they may rarely use. Others prefer to preserve an existing layout and invest more in custom storage and finish details.

Leave room in the budget for conditions that cannot be confirmed until demolition, especially in older Middle Tennessee homes. A careful remodeling partner will explain where uncertainty may exist rather than promising a number that only works if everything behind the walls is perfect. Clear allowances, documented selections, and honest conversations early on are the best protection against unpleasant surprises later.

Build the Layout Before Choosing Finishes

A bathroom layout should support comfortable movement and practical access. That means checking more than whether each fixture technically fits. Consider door swings, shower entry, clearance around the toilet, where a vanity drawer opens, and whether two people can use the room without constantly stepping aside.

Keeping plumbing in roughly the same locations can control costs, but it is not always the right choice. If the existing layout wastes valuable floor space or creates a cramped shower, relocating one fixture may deliver a much better long-term result. The decision depends on the home’s structure, plumbing access, budget, and how long you plan to enjoy the remodeled space.

Storage deserves the same attention as the shower and tile. A well-designed vanity can include deep drawers for styling tools, divided organizers, pullout storage, and a dedicated place for linens. Custom cabinetry is especially valuable in rooms with unusual dimensions or homeowners who want furniture-quality details. For a more budget-conscious remodel, carefully selected stock or RTA cabinetry can still create a polished, functional result when it is properly planned and installed.

Plan for Real Morning Routines

If two people regularly get ready at the same time, a double vanity is not automatically the answer. Two well-spaced sinks may be helpful, but a single larger sink with generous counter space can work better in a narrower room. Consider where outlets belong, whether each person needs dedicated drawer storage, and how mirrors and lighting will serve both users.

In a guest bath, durability and easy cleaning may take priority over elaborate storage. In a family bath, a tub-shower combination and hardwearing surfaces might make more sense than a large walk-in shower. Good planning respects the difference between a room designed for photographs and a room designed for real life.

Make Materials Decisions With Maintenance in Mind

A bathroom is exposed to humidity, splashes, cleaning products, and daily wear. Beautiful materials should also be appropriate for the conditions. Porcelain tile is a popular choice for floors and shower walls because it is durable, versatile, and relatively easy to maintain. Natural stone can bring character and warmth, but it may require more regular sealing and careful cleaning.

For vanity cabinetry, construction quality matters. Bathrooms need materials that stand up to moisture and hinges and drawer hardware that perform reliably over time. Solid wood cabinetry offers lasting strength and a refined appearance, while quality engineered components can be a sensible choice depending on the design and budget. The key is understanding exactly what you are receiving, rather than assuming all cabinets are built alike.

Choose finishes as a coordinated group. Flooring, wall tile, vanity color, countertop, hardware, mirrors, and lighting should each have a role. A calm, timeless foundation often gives you more flexibility than chasing every trend. If you love a bolder look, consider using it in wallpaper, a powder-room vanity, light fixtures, or an accent tile area that can be updated more easily in the future.

Do Not Treat Lighting as an Afterthought

One ceiling fixture rarely provides enough useful bathroom lighting. A comfortable, flattering room typically needs a combination of ambient lighting for overall visibility, task lighting at the mirror, and accent lighting for atmosphere. Sconces at face height can reduce harsh shadows, while a properly positioned vanity light may be the better option when space is limited.

Ask for dimmers where they make sense. Bright light is useful for shaving, makeup, and cleaning, while softer light can make an evening bath feel far more restful. Also plan outlet locations early, including outlets inside a vanity drawer or cabinet if that would help keep electric toothbrushes and grooming tools off the counter.

Ventilation is equally important. A properly sized, quiet exhaust fan protects paint, cabinetry, and finishes from excess moisture. It is not the most glamorous selection in the room, but it is one of the choices that helps the bathroom stay beautiful longer.

Prepare for the Remodeling Process

The construction phase is easier when expectations are set before work begins. Ask who will be your primary point of contact, how changes will be approved, when materials need to be selected, and what parts of the home may be affected by dust, deliveries, or worker access. A thoughtful project plan should address protection for adjacent spaces as well as the sequence of demolition, rough work, installation, finishes, and final details.

If this is your only full bathroom, make a temporary plan before construction starts. Some families schedule work during travel, arrange access to another bathroom in the home, or phase the project when possible. The right approach depends on the scope, but it is far less stressful to solve this early than to scramble after demolition.

When reviewing an estimate, look beyond the bottom line. Confirm what is included for demolition, plumbing, electrical work, tile installation, cabinetry, countertops, fixtures, painting, permits, and cleanup. Detailed planning is not paperwork for its own sake. It is how homeowners maintain control of their budget and how skilled craftspeople deliver work that meets the standard promised.

Choose a Partner Who Brings Clarity

A bathroom remodel involves many decisions, but you should not have to become an expert in every trade to make good ones. Look for a local team that listens closely, explains the options in plain language, and can connect design choices to cost, performance, and installation requirements. The goal is not pressure. It is a plan you can understand and feel good about.

For homeowners in Nashville, Brentwood, Franklin, Belle Meade, and throughout Middle Tennessee, Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom brings cabinetry knowledge, refined craftsmanship, and straightforward project planning to the process. Whether the right solution is fully custom woodwork or a carefully planned budget-conscious update, the finished bathroom should feel considered from the inside of the drawers to the last tile detail.

A well-planned bathroom remodel is an investment in calmer mornings, more comfortable routines, and a home that reflects your taste. Begin with the problems you want solved, make room for honest budget conversations, and choose details that will serve you well long after the excitement of new finishes has settled into everyday life.

Storage Built for Your Space

Pantries, vanities, mudroom lockers, and window seats: we design and build custom built-ins for Nashville homes, scribed to fit walls that are rarely square. Pair them with custom cabinetry or custom millwork and trim for a consistent look room to room.

excerpt: See kitchen cabinet color trends that bring warmth, contrast, and lasting value to Nashville homes, with guidance for a kitchen that feels like your home.
content:
A cabinet color can change the entire feeling of a kitchen before a single appliance is replaced. The kitchen cabinet color trends homeowners are choosing now are less about chasing a fleeting look and more about creating rooms that feel warm, grounded, and personal. For Nashville, Brentwood, and Franklin homes, that often means moving beyond all-white cabinetry while still choosing finishes that will look right for years to come.

The best color for your kitchen is not simply the one appearing most often in design photos. It is the one that works with your home’s natural light, existing flooring, architecture, and the way your family actually uses the room. A thoughtful plan makes it possible to bring in current style without turning a major investment into a dated one.

Kitchen Cabinet Color Trends Moving Beyond White

White cabinets are not disappearing. They remain a smart choice for many kitchens because they reflect light, make a compact room feel more open, and suit a wide range of countertops and backsplashes. But the bright, stark white kitchen is giving way to softer shades with more depth.

Warm whites, creamy off-whites, and light greige finishes are especially appealing in Middle Tennessee homes. These colors still provide the clean, open quality homeowners value, but they feel more welcoming alongside warm wood floors, brass hardware, natural stone, and layered lighting. A soft white also tends to be more forgiving than a crisp, cool white when the kitchen receives limited natural light.

The trade-off is subtle but real. Warmer whites can look yellow when paired with a very cool countertop or gray backsplash. Before choosing a paint or stain, view large samples next to your countertop, flooring, and wall color at different times of day. Morning light, afternoon sun, and overhead lighting can all shift the way a cabinet finish reads.

Earthy Greens Bring Calm and Character

Muted green cabinetry has become one of the strongest kitchen cabinet color trends because it brings color into the room without demanding all the attention. Think soft sage, olive, moss, and gray-green rather than bright emerald. These tones feel at home with the trees, stone, and traditional-meets-modern architecture found throughout Nashville-area neighborhoods.

Green works particularly well on an island, a built-in pantry, or a lower cabinet run paired with a lighter upper cabinet. It creates a focal point while keeping the kitchen from feeling closed in. In a larger space, a deeper olive or forest-inspired green can look refined and timeless when balanced by warm white walls and natural wood accents.

Cabinet construction matters here. A rich painted color will highlight every door profile, joint, and finish detail. Well-built cabinets with precise installation give a saturated shade the polished appearance it deserves. On lower-quality surfaces, dark or heavily pigmented paint can reveal wear and imperfections more quickly.

Where Green Works Best

If you enjoy color but hesitate to commit, begin with the island or a single statement wall of cabinetry. This approach keeps the overall palette flexible and lets the color support the room rather than dominate it. For homeowners who want a more tailored look, green perimeter cabinets paired with a natural wood island can create the kind of depth often seen in custom-designed kitchens.

Blue Is Becoming Softer and More Livable

Navy has had a long run in kitchen design, and it still has a place in the right home. Yet softer blues are taking more of the spotlight. Dusty blue, blue-gray, slate, and muted denim offer contrast without making the room feel formal or overly dramatic.

These shades pair beautifully with honed marble looks, white quartz, brushed nickel, aged brass, and light oak. They can also complement traditional homes where homeowners want an updated kitchen without losing the character that made them love the house in the first place.

Deep navy remains a strong option for an island or beverage station, especially in a kitchen with generous natural light. Just be realistic about maintenance. Darker painted cabinets show dust, fingerprints, and small scratches more readily than mid-tone finishes. For busy family kitchens, a softened blue or blue-gray may offer a similar visual impact with less day-to-day fuss.

Natural Wood Is Back, With a More Refined Look

Natural wood cabinetry is no longer limited to rustic kitchens or heavily orange stains. Current wood finishes favor clean grain, warm medium tones, white oak, walnut, and understated stains that allow the material to speak for itself. This is a meaningful shift for homeowners who want a kitchen with texture, permanence, and a connection to real craftsmanship.

Wood is especially effective when used to break up a painted kitchen. A wood island, floating shelves, range hood surround, or tall pantry section can add warmth to white, green, or blue cabinetry. In a fully wood kitchen, mixing door styles and finishes carefully can prevent the room from feeling too heavy.

The species, stain, and sheen all matter. White oak can read calm and contemporary, while walnut has deeper contrast and a more formal presence. A clear or low-sheen finish usually feels more current than a glossy surface, but it also needs to be selected for durability and cleanability. The goal is not merely to follow a trend. It is to choose a material that will age gracefully in a hardworking room.

Two-Tone Cabinets Create Intentional Contrast

Two-tone kitchens remain popular because they solve a practical design challenge: they add visual interest without requiring every cabinet to be a bold color. The most dependable approach is light upper cabinets with darker lowers or a darker island. This keeps the room visually open while grounding it at floor level.

A warm white perimeter with a stained wood or muted green island is one of the most adaptable combinations available. It works in newer homes, remodeled traditional kitchens, and spaces where homeowners want a custom look while staying mindful of budget. Another option is wood lowers with creamy painted uppers, which can make the kitchen feel both architectural and inviting.

The key is restraint. Two tones should look connected by a shared undertone, countertop, or hardware finish. For example, cool gray cabinets beside a yellow-toned wood floor can feel disconnected unless another element bridges the gap. A professional design plan helps identify these details before cabinets are ordered and installed.

Dark Cabinets Are Best Used With Purpose

Charcoal, near-black, and deep espresso cabinets can be striking, but they are not right for every kitchen. They create drama, define a large open-concept room, and look exceptional against light stone countertops. In a kitchen with ample windows, dark cabinetry can feel sophisticated rather than heavy.

In a smaller or low-light room, however, dark cabinets can absorb light and make the space feel tighter. That does not mean they are off the table. A dark island, lower cabinets, or a built-in hutch can provide the same richness without overwhelming the room. Adding under-cabinet lighting and choosing a lighter backsplash also makes a significant difference.

Homeowners should also consider their preferred level of upkeep. A matte charcoal finish often disguises fingerprints better than glossy black, but no dark color is completely maintenance-free. Your kitchen should support real life, not make you worry every time someone reaches for a snack.

How to Choose a Color You Will Still Love Later

Trend awareness is useful, but longevity comes from designing around your home rather than a showroom display. Start with the fixed elements that are least likely to change: floors, countertops, window light, adjacent rooms, and architectural details. Then choose cabinet color as part of the whole composition.

It also helps to separate a lasting cabinet finish from easily updated accents. A soft neutral, natural wood, or muted blue-green can provide a durable foundation. Hardware, pendants, stools, wall paint, and decor can carry more of the seasonal personality. This approach protects your investment while still allowing the kitchen to evolve.

At Tom Bell Cabinetry & Custom, the design conversation begins with how you want the room to feel and function, not with pressure to choose the most expensive option. Whether a project calls for fully custom solid wood cabinetry or a budget-conscious cabinet solution, clear planning makes color decisions easier and helps avoid costly surprises once work begins.

A well-chosen cabinet color should make you pause at the kitchen doorway and feel glad you are home. Choose the finish that suits your light, your family, and your house, then give it the craftsmanship and planning needed to make that feeling last.
